metadata.scope: e_tibet (all baronies across k_amdo, k_guge, k_gyalrong, k_kham, k_lhomon, k_maryul, k_tsang, and k_u)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_gonghe.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. 'Gonghe' (共和, 'Republic') is a 20th-century Mandarin Chinese administrative name, while the county seat name 'Aksay' (阿克塞) dates to the 1954 CE establishment of the Aksay Kazakh Autonomous Region/County.
b_gonghe.etymology_analysis: From Mandarin Chinese 共和 (Gònghé, 'republic'), a 20th-century political/administrative toponym; in-game localized as Aksay (from Kazakh Aqsay, 'pure/white ravine', adopted in 1954 CE).

b_tuanjie.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. 'Tuanjie' (团结, 'Unity') is a modern 20th-century PRC-era Mandarin Chinese place name.
b_tuanjie.etymology_analysis: From Mandarin Chinese 团结 (Tuánjié, 'unity / solidarity'), a modern PRC-era ideological settlement/peak name.

b_dahaleteng.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. 'Dahaleteng' (大哈尔腾河, Big Haltang River) is attested only in modern Qinghai/Gansu geographical surveys.
b_dahaleteng.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Mandarin Chinese + Mongolic/Turkic hydronym meaning 'Big Haltang' (大哈尔腾), referring to the endorheic river flowing from Delingha into Aksay.

b_takoerpasitao.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. 'Takoerpasitao' (塔喀尔巴斯陶) is a Kazakh-derived spring/stream name along the Haltang River in Aksay, reflecting 20th-century Kazakh settlement in Gansu.
b_takoerpasitao.etymology_analysis: Mandarin transliteration (塔喀尔巴斯陶) of Kazakh Taqır-bastaw ('barren-flat spring'), referring to the resurgent springs of the Haltang River in Aksay.

b_amdo.first_mention_attestation: The specific form 'Amdo' (ཨ་མདོ་, a mdo) became common only in the 19th century (ca. 1801 CE onward); 9th-century Dunhuang Tibetan manuscripts instead refer to the northeastern Tibetan region as mdo-smad (Domey) and mdo-gams (Do Kham), while Amdo County in Nagqu is a modern PRC administrative unit.
b_amdo.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཨ་མདོ་ (a mdo), with dialectal prefix a- attached to mdo ('lower valley/confluence', related to older mdo-smad / Domey).

historical_names.name: Mdo-smad
historical_names.source: Old Tibetan Dunhuang manuscripts (9th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Dunhuang manuscripts from the Tibetan Empire period refer to northeastern Tibet as mdo-smad (Domey) and mdo-gams, whereas the specific form 'Amdo' (a mdo) became widespread only in the 19th century.

historical_names.name: Mdo-gams
historical_names.source: Old Tibetan Dunhuang manuscripts (9th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Dunhuang manuscripts from the Tibetan Empire period refer to northeastern Tibet as mdo-smad (Domey) and mdo-gams, whereas the specific form 'Amdo' (a mdo) became widespread only in the 19th century.

b_gangnyi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Gangnyi (岗尼乡) is a modern township-level division of Amdo County, Nagqu, Tibet Autonomous Region.
b_gangnyi.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan, likely gangs nyi ('snowy sun' or 'two snow peaks' / sgang gnyis 'two ridges'), used for a modern pastoral township in Amdo County.

b_sibnak_chenchungo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. No pre-867 CE written attestation exists for Sibnak Chenchungo.
b_sibnak_chenchungo.etymology_analysis: Compound Tibetan toponym combining srib nag ('dark shady slope') and chen chung mgo ('great-small summit/head').

b_aqenganggyai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. 'Aqênganggyai' (阿卿贡嘉) is the Tibetan name for the Hoh Xil region/mountains, documented only in modern geographical literature.
b_aqenganggyai.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan, meaning 'Lord of Ten Thousand Mountains' / 'Great Snow-Mountain King', the Tibetan name for the Hoh Xil range.

b_ulenulaco.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Ulan Ula Lake (乌兰乌拉湖) is a remote endorheic lake in Hoh Xil attested only in modern surveys.
b_ulenulaco.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Mongolian-Tibetan hydronym combining Mongolian Ulaγan Aγula ('Red Mountain') with Tibetan mtsho ('lake').

b_drakbuk.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Lake Drakbuk (བྲག་སྦུག་མཚོ།, brag sbug mtsho) is attested only in modern Tibetan Plateau gazetteers.
b_drakbuk.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan བྲག་སྦུག (brag sbug, 'rock hollow / cave recess'), referring to Lake Drakbuk in the northern Tibetan Plateau.

b_chumarho.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. The Chumar River (楚玛尔河, Tibetan chu dmar) is attested only in post-867 CE geographical records.
b_chumarho.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Tibetan-Chinese hydronym from Tibetan chu dmar ('Red Water') + Mandarin hé ('river'), a northern headwater of the Yangtze.

b_nengyi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. No pre-867 CE written attestation exists for Nengyi.
b_nengyi.etymology_analysis: Romanized local Tibetan toponym in the Chumar River area without a documented pre-867 CE attestation.

b_dangla.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. The Dangla / Tanggula Mountains (གདང་ལ་, gdang la) are attested only in later Tibetan/Qing-era and modern geographical sources.
b_dangla.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan གདང་ལ (gdang la), referring to the major mountain pass and range dividing Qinghai and central Tibet.

b_marchu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Marchu (玛曲乡) is a modern township administered by Amdo County.
b_marchu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan mar chu / rma chu ('lower/ochre river'), a local river and modern township in Amdo County.

b_quemoco.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Quemo Co (雀莫错) is a saline lake in Tanggulashan Town, Golmud, attested only in modern surveys.
b_quemoco.etymology_analysis: Tibetan hydronym ending in mtsho ('lake', Sinicized as cuo/co), located in the Zurken Ula basin near the Yangtze headwaters.

b_nyainrong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Nyainrong (གཉན་རོང་, gnyan rong) is attested only in post-867 CE Tibetan and modern county records.
b_nyainrong.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan གཉན་རོང (gnyan rong, 'argali/nyen-spirit valley'), the name of Nyainrong County in Nagqu.

b_marrong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Marrong (དམར་རོང, dmar rong) is a modern township in Amdo County, Nagqu.

b_yenshipin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Yanshiping (雁石坪镇) is a modern Chinese-named town along the Qinghai-Tibet Highway.
b_yenshipin.etymology_analysis: From Mandarin Chinese 雁石坪 (Yànshípíng, 'Wild-Goose Stone Flat'), a modern highway settlement administered by Amdo County.

b_changco.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. No pre-867 CE written attestation exists for Changco.
b_changco.etymology_analysis: Tibetan directional compound byang mtsho ('Northern Lake'), unattested by 867 CE.

b_hohaseco.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Hoh Xil Lake (可可西里湖) is a Mongolic-Tibetan hydronym post-dating Mongol presence in Qinghai.
b_hohaseco.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Mongolian-Tibetan hydronym combining Mongolian köke sil ('blue ridge') with Tibetan mtsho ('lake').

b_ragbangadung.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Ragba'ngadung is a remote lake in Qinghai attested only in modern cartographic databases.
b_ragbangadung.etymology_analysis: Tibetan-origin lake name in Qinghai Province without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_ayakkum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Lake Ayakkum (ئاياققۇم كۆلى) is attested only in modern cartographic and geological surveys.
b_ayakkum.etymology_analysis: From Uyghur Ayaqqum ('foot/lower end of the sands'), a saline lake in the Kumkol Basin of Ruoqiang County, Xinjiang.

b_aqqikkol.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Lake Aqqikkol (阿其克库勒湖) is attested only in modern cartographic surveys.
b_aqqikkol.etymology_analysis: From Uyghur Achchiq-köl ('bitter/saline lake'), a closed-basin saline lake in Ruoqiang County, Xinjiang.

b_kytkol.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Kytkol (Kichik Kumköl / 克其克库木库勒湖) is attested only in modern surveys.
b_kytkol.etymology_analysis: Abbreviated form of Uyghur Kichik Kumköl ('Small Sand Lake'), in the Kumkol Basin of Ruoqiang County.

b_lenghu.first_mention_attestation: Formerly uninhabited desert; Lenghu (冷湖, 'Cold Lake') was founded in 1954 CE following oil discovery in the northern Qaidam Basin.
b_lenghu.etymology_analysis: From Mandarin Chinese 冷湖 (Lěnghú, 'Cold Lake'), named in 1954 CE after a nearby cold salt lake.

b_urtmoron.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Urt Moron (乌图美仁) is a Mongolian hydronym post-dating Mongol entry into Qaidam; the modern township was established in 1961 CE (renamed Urtmoron in 1984 CE).
b_urtmoron.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian urtu müren ('long river'), referring to a river in the southern Qaidam Basin near Golmud.

b_qaidam.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. 'Qaidam' (柴达木) is a Mongolian choronym post-dating Mongol settlement in Qinghai (13th–17th centuries CE).
b_qaidam.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian čayidam ('salt marsh / broad alkali basin'), referring to the Qaidam Basin in northwestern Qinghai.

b_mangnai.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Qing Dynasty records in 1725 CE (Yongzheng 3rd year); the modern city of Mangnai was formed in 2018 CE.
b_mangnai.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian mangnai ('forehead'), referring to the forehead-shaped yardang ridges in the western Qaidam Basin.

b_bokalik.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Bokalik Tagh / Bukadaban Feng (博卡雷克塔格山) is attested only in modern geographical surveys.
b_bokalik.etymology_analysis: From Uyghur Buka-lik ('place of wild bulls/yaks'), an alternate name for Bukadaban Feng, the highest peak in Qinghai.

b_nagormo.first_mention_attestation: Golmud / Nagormo (格尔木) was first established as a settlement in 1954 CE during construction of the Qinghai-Tibet Highway; the Mongolian toponym post-dates 867 CE.
b_nagormo.etymology_analysis: Tibetanized/transliterated as Nagormo from Mongolian Golmud (γool-mud, 'many rivers / river-dense place').

b_dagelhe.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Dagele Township (大格勒乡) is a modern administrative division of Golmud.
b_dagelhe.etymology_analysis: Modern Mandarin rendering (大格勒) of a Mongolic toponym in the eastern Golmud area.

b_zhiteu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Zhidoi / Drito (འབྲི་སྟོད་, 'bri stod) was established as a county in 1953 CE and lacks pre-867 CE attestation.
b_zhiteu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan འབྲི་སྟོད ('bri stod, 'upper reaches of the Drichu/Yangtze'), a directional/locator compound.

b_triwang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Triwang is a modern/Qinghai Tibetan place in Chindu (Trindu) County without pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_triwang.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan khri dbang ('myriad/throne power'), a settlement in Chindu County, Yushu Prefecture.

b_damda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Damda (འདམ་མདའ།, Qingshuihe Town) in Chindu County is attested only in modern gazetteers.
b_damda.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan འདམ་མདའ ('dam mda', 'lower marsh valley'), a town in Chindu County.

b_ngoring.first_mention_attestation: The name Ngoring / Eling (鄂陵湖) is attested in Qing Dynasty Yellow River source surveys (1704 CE); Tang Dynasty records (641 CE) instead attest the name Baihai (柏海) for the lake(s) at the Yellow River headwaters.
b_ngoring.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan mtsho sngo ring ('long blue lake'), one of the two large freshwater lakes in the upper Yellow River basin.

historical_names.name: Baihai
historical_names.source: Tang Dynasty histories (641 CE meeting of Songtsen Gampo and Princess Wencheng at Baihai)
historical_names.notes: Tang Dynasty Chinese sources (641 CE) record the Yellow River headwater lake(s) as Baihai (柏海); the Tibetan name Ngoring (Eling) is attested later in Qing-era surveys.

b_mato.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Madoi / Matö (རྨ་སྟོད།) is a modern county/township name in Golog TAP, Qinghai.
b_mato.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan རྨ་སྟོད (rma stod, 'upper reaches of the Yellow River'), a directional/locator compound.

b_qumarleb.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Qumarlêb (ཆུ་དམར་ལེབ་) is a modern county in Yushu TAP, Qinghai.
b_qumarleb.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཆུ་དམར་ལེབ (chu dmar leb, 'Red River plain/flat').

b_chikdril.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Chikdril / Jigzhi County (གཅིག་སྒྲིལ་) was established in 1955 CE.
b_chikdril.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan གཅིག་སྒྲིལ (gcig sgril, 'united as one'), a 20th-century administrative name for Jigzhi County.

b_derlenka.first_mention_attestation: Delingha (德令哈) was established as an administrative work committee in 1955 CE (county in 1958 CE); the Mongolian name Altan Delkhei post-dates 867 CE.
b_derlenka.etymology_analysis: From Mongolian Altan Delkhei ('golden world'), the seat of Haixi Mongol and Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture.

b_conak.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. No pre-867 CE written attestation exists for Conak.

b_ngor.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE. Ngor (ངོར་) is associated in Tibetan Buddhism with Ngor Monastery founded in 1429 CE, and is unattested in Delingha by 867 CE.
b_ngor.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ངོར (ngor), a Tibetan monastic toponym (famous from the 15th-century Ngor Monastery of the Sakya school).

b_fuqi.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Fusi City (伏俟城, also read Fuqicheng), built around 540 CE by the Tuyuhun ruler Fulianchou/Kualü near Qinghai Lake and recorded in the Book of Wei and Book of Sui.

morphemes.translation: prostrate, submit (phonetic transcription of Xianbei/Tuyuhun royal name)

b_fuqi.etymology_analysis: Chinese transcription (伏俟城 Fúsìchéng / Fúqíchéng) of the royal capital of the Tuyuhun Kingdom established west of Qinghai Lake in the mid-6th century CE.

b_temqen.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Temqen (Tianjun County, 天峻县), a modern administrative division in Haixi Prefecture established in the 20th century.
b_temqen.etymology_analysis: Tibetan/Mongolic phonetic adaptation (Têmqên / Them chen) of Mandarin Tianjun (天峻, 'lofty/steep'), a modern county name in Haixi Prefecture.

b_yagkeng.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Yagkeng as a settlement name.
b_yagkeng.etymology_analysis: Local Amdo Tibetan toponym in the Qinghai Lake basin without documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_gangca.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Gangca (Tibetan: rkang tsha; Chinese: 刚察), a modern county on the northern shore of Qinghai Lake.

morphemes.translation: foot, base, or tribe name element

b_gangca.etymology_analysis: Tibetan toponym (རྐང་ཚ་ rkang tsha), adapted into Chinese as Gangcha (刚察), used for the modern county north of Qinghai Lake.

b_qabqa.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Qabqa (Chabcha, 恰卜恰), the modern seat of Gonghe County; the surrounding Gonghe basin was recorded as Dafeichuan (大非川) in 670 CE.
b_qabqa.etymology_analysis: Tibetan toponym Chabcha (ཆབ་ཆ་, transcribed Qabqa / Qiabuqia), modern county seat of Gonghe in Hainan Prefecture, Qinghai.

historical_names.name: Dafeichuan
historical_names.source: Old Book of Tang (Battle of Dafeichuan, 670 CE)
historical_names.notes: Tang-Tibetan Battle of Dafeichuan in 670 CE took place in modern Gonghe County.

b_changzhi.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Changzhi as a settlement in Qinghai.
b_changzhi.etymology_analysis: Chinese-form settlement name in the game's Qinghai setup with no pre-867 CE written attestation in this region.

b_haeyan.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Haeyan (Haiyan County, 海晏县), a modern county on the northeast shore of Qinghai Lake.
b_haeyan.etymology_analysis: Tibetan phonetic rendering (Ha'eyan, ཧའེ་ཡན་) of Chinese Haiyan (海晏, 'tranquil lake/sea'), a modern county name.

b_tuulain.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the Mongolic name Tuulain / Dulan (都兰); although the Dulan/Reshui area contains 7th-8th century Tuyuhun-Tubo tombs, the name itself is post-867 CE.
b_tuulain.etymology_analysis: From Mongolic dulaɣan ('warm'), adapted into Tibetan as Tu'ulain (ཏུའུ་ལན་) and Chinese as Dulan (都兰).

b_balung_dulan.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Balung Dulan (Balong Township, 巴隆乡, Dulan County); Bronze Age Nuomuhong ruins exist locally but without a recorded ancient name.
b_balung_dulan.etymology_analysis: Compound of Balong/Balung (a modern township in Dulan County) and Dulan (Mongolic 'warm').

b_ulam.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Ulam (Ulan / Wulan County, 乌兰县), a Mongolic toponym in Haixi Prefecture.
b_ulam.etymology_analysis: From Mongolic ulaɣan ('red'), adapted into Chinese as Wulan (乌兰) and Tibetanized as Ulam.

b_cakha.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Cakha (Chaka, 茶卡), the salt-lake settlement in Ulan County.
b_cakha.etymology_analysis: Tibetan tshwa kha (ཚྭ་ཁ་, 'salt lake / salt pan'), referring to Chaka Salt Lake in Ulan County, Qinghai.

b_xigortang.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Xigortang (Ziketan, seat of Xinghai County, Hainan Prefecture).
b_xigortang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan toponym ending in thang ('plain'), corresponding to Ziketan (子科滩), the seat of Xinghai County.

b_namtang.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Namtang.
b_namtang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan compound gnam thang ('sky plain'), a descriptive highland steppe toponym without pre-867 CE attestation.

b_datong.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Datong (大通) in Qinghai; the administrative name Datong dates to the Qing dynasty (Datong Guard, 1724 CE).
b_datong.etymology_analysis: Chinese name Dàtōng (大通, 'great passage/unity'), used for the Qing-era garrison and modern autonomous county north of Xining.

b_serkok.first_mention_attestation: Serkok Monastery (Tibetan: gser khog dgon pa; Chinese: Guanghui Si, 广惠寺) in Datong County was founded in 1650 CE.
b_serkok.etymology_analysis: Tibetan gser khog ('golden valley'), the Tibetan name of Guanghui Monastery in Datong County, founded in 1650 CE.

b_rusar_huangzhong.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for the combined name Rusar Huangzhong; Huangzhong County was named in 1943 CE when its seat moved to Lushar (Rusar), though the Han dynasty established Linqiang here and Huangzhong is attested by 394 CE.
b_rusar_huangzhong.etymology_analysis: Hybrid of Lushar/Rusar (the town beside Kumbum Monastery, founded 1583 CE) and Huangzhong ('middle Huangshui valley').

historical_names.name: Linqiang
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Western Han Linqiang County under Jincheng Commandery, c. 61 BCE) and Former Qin records (Huangzhong, 394 CE)
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty established Linqiang County here; Huangzhong is attested in Former Qin records (394 CE).

historical_names.name: Huangzhong
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Western Han Linqiang County under Jincheng Commandery, c. 61 BCE) and Former Qin records (Huangzhong, 394 CE)
historical_names.notes: Han dynasty established Linqiang County here; Huangzhong is attested in Former Qin records (394 CE).

b_xining.first_mention_attestation: Recovered by the Northern Song dynasty in 1104 CE and renamed Xining (西宁, 'Peace in the West').
b_xining.etymology_analysis: Chinese Xīníng (西宁, 'Peace in the West'), bestowed by the Northern Song court in 1104 CE.

historical_names.name: Xipingting
historical_names.source: Han dynasty records (Xiping Pavilion, 121 BCE); Northern Wei/Tang records (Shanzhou, 526 CE)
historical_names.notes: Established as Xiping Pavilion in 121 BCE; renamed Shanzhou in 526 CE before Song renamed it Xining in 1104 CE.

historical_names.name: Shanzhou
historical_names.source: Han dynasty records (Xiping Pavilion, 121 BCE); Northern Wei/Tang records (Shanzhou, 526 CE)
historical_names.notes: Established as Xiping Pavilion in 121 BCE; renamed Shanzhou in 526 CE before Song renamed it Xining in 1104 CE.

b_tongkor.first_mention_attestation: Tongkor Monastery (Tibetan: stong 'khor dgon) was established near Dangar (Huangyuan) in 1648 CE.
b_tongkor.etymology_analysis: Tibetan stong 'khor (སྟོང་འཁོར་), the monastic lineage and monastery established near Dangar (Huangyuan) in 1648 CE.

b_trandam.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Trandam (Chindu / Chenduo, 称多) in Yushu Prefecture.
b_trandam.etymology_analysis: Tibetan khri 'du (ཁྲི་འདུ་, 'gathering of ten thousand'), rendered in Chinese as Chenduo/Chindu and in-game as Trandam.

b_damzhung.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Damzhung in Yushu Prefecture.

b_toma.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Toma in Yushu Prefecture.
b_toma.etymology_analysis: Tibetan toponym (stod ma, 'upper') in the Trandam/Chindu area without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_qapugtang.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Qapugtang (Sahuteng, 萨呼腾), the modern county seat of Zadoi County (renamed Qapugtang Town in 2001 CE).
b_qapugtang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan bya phug thang (བྱ་ཕུག་ཐང་, 'bird-cave plain'), transcribed as Qapugtang / Sahuteng.

b_ato.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Ato (Aduo Township, 阿多乡) in Zadoi County.
b_ato.etymology_analysis: Tibetan a stod (ཨ་སྟོད་, transcribed Ato / Aduo), a modern township in Zadoi County, Qinghai.

b_mukzhung.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Mukzhung (Moyun Township, 莫云乡) in Zadoi County.
b_mukzhung.etymology_analysis: Tibetan smug gzhung (སྨུག་གཞུང་, 'misty valley'), transcribed as Mukzhung / Moyun.

b_gyaijepozhangge.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Gyaijepozhangge (Jiajiboluoge Town, 加吉博洛格镇), the modern seat of Zhidoi County.
b_gyaijepozhangge.etymology_analysis: Tibetan toponym transcribed in Chinese as Jiajiboluoge (加吉博洛格), the modern county seat of Zhidoi.

b_drakgur.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Drakgur (Chaggar/Zhahe Township, 扎河乡) in Zhidoi County.
b_drakgur.etymology_analysis: Tibetan brag dkar / brag dgur ('white rock / bent crag'), a modern township in Zhidoi County.

b_zokya.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Zokya (Suojia Township, 索加乡) in Zhidoi County.
b_zokya.etymology_analysis: Tibetan zo skya (ཟོ་སྐྱ་, transcribed Zokya / Suojia), a modern township in Zhidoi County.

b_gar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Gar (sgar) as a settlement; Gartok (Gar Günsa / Gar Yarsa) became Lhasa's administrative headquarters for Ngari after 1684 CE.
b_gar.etymology_analysis: Tibetan sgar (སྒར་, 'encampment'), referring to the seasonal encampments of Gartok in western Tibet.

b_zoco.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Zoco (Tsotso / Zuozuo Township, 左左乡) in Gar County, Ngari.
b_zoco.etymology_analysis: Tibetan gtso tsho (གཙོ་ཚོ་, transcribed Zoco / Zuozuo), a modern township in Gar County.

b_gegyai.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Gegyai (Gê'gyai County, 革吉县) in Ngari Prefecture.
b_gegyai.etymology_analysis: Tibetan dge rgyas (དགེ་རྒྱས་, 'full beauty / flourishing virtue'), transcribed as Gê'gyai / Geji.

b_xungba.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Xungba (Xiongba Township, 雄巴乡) in Gê'gyai County, Ngari.
b_xungba.etymology_analysis: Tibetan toponym transcribed as Xungba / Xiongba, a modern township in Gê'gyai County.

b_chaka.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Chaka (Yanhu, salt lake settlement) in Gê'gyai County, Ngari.
b_chaka.etymology_analysis: Tibetan tshwa kha (ཚྭ་ཁ་, 'salt lake / salt pan'), corresponding to Yanhu Township in Gê'gyai County.

b_gerze.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Gerze (Gêrzê / Gertse County, 改则县); the county government was established in 1960 CE.
b_gerze.etymology_analysis: Tibetan sger rtse (སྒེར་རྩེ་), referring to a local style of mountain-peak dwelling/clan name in Ngari.

b_dongco.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Dongco (Tong Tso, 洞错) in Gêrzê County.
b_dongco.etymology_analysis: Tibetan stong mtsho (སྟོང་མཚོ་, 'Dongco / Tong Tso'), a salt lake and township in Gêrzê County.

b_chagboco.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Chagboco (Chabu Township, 察布乡) in Gêrzê County.
b_chagboco.etymology_analysis: Tibetan hydronym/toponym ending in mtsho ('lake'), corresponding to Chabu in Gêrzê County.

b_gomoco.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Gomoco (Gomo Co, 戈木错) in Gêrzê County.
b_gomoco.etymology_analysis: Tibetan hydronym Gomo Co (mtsho = 'lake') in the Changtang plateau of Gêrzê County.

b_burogco.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE found for Burogco (Burog Co, 布若错) in northern Gêrzê County.
b_burogco.etymology_analysis: Tibetan hydronym Burog Co (mtsho = 'lake'), a high-altitude glacial lake in northern Ngari.

b_kyunglung.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written or epigraphic attestation <= 867 CE; later Bonpo and post-imperial Tibetan traditions retrospectively identify Khyunglung Ngulkhar as the 7th-century CE (c. 625–645 CE) Zhangzhung capital.
b_kyunglung.etymology_analysis: Tibetan khyung lung (ཁྱུང་ལུང་, 'Garuda Valley'), the ancient capital of Zhangzhung in the upper Sutlej valley.

b_monicer.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Minsar / Moincêr (མོན་འཚེར), held as a treaty enclave of the Kingdom of Ladakh from 1684 CE.
b_monicer.etymology_analysis: Tibetan mon 'tsher (མོན་འཚེར་, 'Mon settlement'), also known as Minsar or Menshi, southwest of Mount Kailash.

b_tsaparang.first_mention_attestation: Tsaparang was established as the capital of the Kingdom of Guge in the 10th century CE (c. 950 CE) following the Tibetan Era of Fragmentation.
b_tsaparang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan toponym rtsa pa rangs (རྩ་པ་རངས་), the 10th-century fortress capital of the Guge Kingdom in the upper Sutlej valley.

b_tholing.first_mention_attestation: Tholing Monastery (mtho lding dgon pa) was founded in 997 CE by Yeshe-Ö, the second king of the Guge Kingdom.
b_tholing.etymology_analysis: Tibetan mtho lding (མཐོ་ལྡིང་, 'hovering/soaring high'), named for the high-altitude monastery founded in 997 CE.

b_trashigang.first_mention_attestation: Tashigang (Zhaxigang) in Gar County, Ngari Prefecture, houses a monastery traditionally dated to the 11th century CE and was fortified/rebuilt under Ladakhi ruler Sengge Namgyal in 1630 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_trashigang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan bkra shis sgang means 'auspicious hillock' or 'auspicious ridge', referring to the isolated rock outcrop at the confluence of the Sengge Zangbo and Gartang rivers.

b_busin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical records <= 867 CE; no documented pre-modern or modern settlement by this exact name is attested in Tsaparang/Zanda.
b_busin.etymology_analysis: No verified Tibetan orthography or historical etymology is documented for Busin in the Tsaparang/Zanda area.

b_aso.first_mention_attestation: Aso Township in Nyima County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the region was historically part of the Nacang (Nagtshang) pastoralist territory before coming under Kashag administration in the late 17th century CE and Xainza Dzong in 1886 CE.
b_aso.etymology_analysis: Aso (Chinese: 阿索乡) is a modern township-level division in Nyima County, Nagqu, derived from a local Tibetan pastoralist place name without attested pre-867 CE etymology.

b_ngoqu.first_mention_attestation: Ngoqu Township (sngo chu) in Nyima County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Nyima County was carved out of Xainza County in 1983 CE.
b_ngoqu.etymology_analysis: Tibetan sngo chu literally means 'blue river' or 'green stream', a hydronymic toponym adopted for the township in Nyima County.

b_nyima.first_mention_attestation: Nyima (nyi ma) has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the area belonged to the Nacang tribe until Kashag rule in the late 17th century CE and was established as Nyima County in 1983 CE.
b_nyima.etymology_analysis: Tibetan nyi ma means 'sun', used as a modern settlement and county name in Nagqu.

b_ladoi.first_mention_attestation: Ladoi Township in Nyima County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ladoi.etymology_analysis: Tibetan la stod (Ladoi) is a directional/elevation compound meaning 'upper pass'.

b_sinya.first_mention_attestation: Sinya Township in Nyima County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_sinya.etymology_analysis: Sinya (Chinese: 申亚乡) is a township in Nyima County, Nagqu, without attested pre-867 CE written records.

b_gyagog.first_mention_attestation: Gyagog Township (rgya sgog) in Nyima County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_gyagog.etymology_analysis: Gyagog (Wylie: rgya sgog; Chinese: 甲谷乡) is a modern township in Nyima County, Nagqu.

b_xainza.first_mention_attestation: Xainza (shan rtsa) was established as Xainza Dzong by the Tibetan Kashag government in 1886 CE, replacing the earlier Nacang Deba tribal designation.
b_xainza.etymology_analysis: Tibetan shan rtsa means 'in front of the fur-bellows-shaped mountain gully', describing the local valley topography.

b_shyungme.first_mention_attestation: Shyungme Town (gzhung smad) in Xainza County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_shyungme.etymology_analysis: Tibetan gzhung smad (Shyungme, Chinese: 雄梅镇) is a directional/locator compound meaning 'lower central valley'.

b_coqen.first_mention_attestation: Coqen (mtsho chen) has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Coqen County was established in the 20th century CE from parts of Xainza, Ngamring, and neighboring pastoralist areas.
b_coqen.etymology_analysis: Tibetan mtsho chen means 'great lake', named after the nearby salt lake Zhari Namco.

b_qulho.first_mention_attestation: Qulho Township (chu lho) in Coqen County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_qulho.etymology_analysis: Tibetan chu lho (Qulho, Chinese: 曲洛乡) is a directional compound meaning 'south river'.

b_gyesarco.first_mention_attestation: Gyesarco (Gesar Lake) in western Tibet has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_gyesarco.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Tibetan epic name Gesar and mtsho ('lake'), forming a hydronymic place name.

b_cuonaco.first_mention_attestation: Cuonaco (mtsho nag mtsho) has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_cuonaco.etymology_analysis: Tibetan mtsho nag means 'black lake', a hydronymic name in the Tibetan plateau lake region.

b_argogco.first_mention_attestation: Argogco (ar kog mtsho, Arkok Tso) in northeastern Coqen County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_argogco.etymology_analysis: Tibetan ar kog mtsho (Chinese: 阿果错) is a small plateau lake in northeastern Coqen County.

b_lunggar.first_mention_attestation: Lunggar Township (lung dkar) in Zhongba County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_lunggar.etymology_analysis: Tibetan lung dkar means 'white valley', a topographic name for a settlement in Zhongba County.

b_ringtor.first_mention_attestation: Ringtor Township in Zhongba County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ringtor.etymology_analysis: Ringtor (Rintor, Chinese: 仁多乡) is a modern township in Zhongba County, Shigatse, without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_barma.first_mention_attestation: Barma Township (bar ma) in Zhongba County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_barma.etymology_analysis: Tibetan bar ma means 'middle' or 'intermediate', a relative locator term.

b_manthang.first_mention_attestation: Lo Manthang was founded in 1380 CE by Ame Pal as the walled capital of the Kingdom of Lo (Upper Mustang).
b_manthang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan smon thang (Manthang) means 'plain of aspiration', founded as a walled royal capital in 1380 CE.

b_muktinath.first_mention_attestation: The specific Sanskrit name Muktinath is not attested in early texts <= 867 CE (where the site appears as Muktikshetra or in 8th-century CE Tibetan Buddhist tradition as Chumig Gyatsa); the present Muktinath pagoda temple was built in the early 19th century CE.
b_muktinath.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Muktinātha means 'Lord of Liberation', a Hindu epithet of Vishnu at the sacred Mustang shrine.

historical_names.name: Chumig Gyatsa
historical_names.source: Tibetan Buddhist tradition associating Chumig Gyatsa ('Hundred Springs') with Padmasambhava (8th century CE) and Puranic Gandaki Mahatmya references to Muktikshetra.
historical_names.notes: Chumig Gyatsa (Tibetan: chu mig brgya rtsa) and Muktikshetra are the earlier attested names for the sacred site.

historical_names.name: Muktikshetra
historical_names.source: Tibetan Buddhist tradition associating Chumig Gyatsa ('Hundred Springs') with Padmasambhava (8th century CE) and Puranic Gandaki Mahatmya references to Muktikshetra.
historical_names.notes: Chumig Gyatsa (Tibetan: chu mig brgya rtsa) and Muktikshetra are the earlier attested names for the sacred site.

b_dolpo.first_mention_attestation: Dolpo (dol po) appears in historical records since c. the 8th century CE during the Tibetan Yarlung dynasty expansion.
b_dolpo.etymology_analysis: Dolpo (Tibetan: དོལ་པོ) is a historical high-altitude Tibetan cultural region in western Nepal attested from c. the 8th century CE; its root etymology remains uncertain.

b_teglakar.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written or epigraphic attestation <= 867 CE; later local and Tibetan chronicle traditions retrospectively date Tegla Kar to the Zhangzhung period and Songtsen Gampo's 7th-century CE conquest.
b_teglakar.etymology_analysis: Tibetan stag la mkhar (Tegla Kar) means 'Lying Tiger Fort', an ancient Zhangzhung fortress above Purang.

b_simbiling.first_mention_attestation: Simbiling Monastery (Shambuling Gompa) was a Gelugpa monastery above Purang; because the Gelugpa school was founded in 1409 CE, Simbiling post-dates 867 CE.
b_simbiling.etymology_analysis: Simbiling (also Shambuling / Shepeling) was a post-867 CE Gelugpa monastic complex near Tegla Kar in Purang.

b_hor.first_mention_attestation: Hor Township in Purang County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_hor.etymology_analysis: Tibetan hor refers to non-Tibetan northern nomadic groups (originally Turkic in the 9th century CE and later Mongolic); Hor Township in Purang is a modern administrative unit.

b_labrang.first_mention_attestation: Labrang Township (bla brang, Drongpa Township) in Zhongba County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_labrang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan bla brang (Labrang) means 'lama's residence' or monastic estate.

b_baryang.first_mention_attestation: Baryang Town (bar yangs, Paryang) in Zhongba County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_baryang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan bar yangs means 'wide middle' or 'broad intermediate plain', a relative locator compound.

b_penchi.first_mention_attestation: Penchi Township (phen phyi) in Zhongba County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_penchi.etymology_analysis: Penchi (Wylie: phen phyi shang; Chinese: 偏吉乡) is a modern township in Zhongba County, Shigatse.

b_yagra.first_mention_attestation: Yagra Township (yag ra) in Zhongba County has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_yagra.etymology_analysis: Tibetan yag ra (Chinese: 亚热乡) is a village and township in Zhongba County near Mount Kailash.

b_darzedo.first_mention_attestation: Dartsedo (dar rtse mdo, modern Kangding) is documented as a major Sino-Tibetan tea-horse trade center from the Ming/Qing periods (e.g., Battle of Dartsedo in 1701 CE; renamed Kangding in 1904 CE); no specific written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_darzedo.etymology_analysis: Tibetan dar rtse mdo means 'confluence of the Dar and Tse rivers', referring to the river junction where the town developed.

b_shade.first_mention_attestation: Shade Town (sa bde / gsar sde) in Kangding has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_shade.etymology_analysis: Tibetan sa bde means 'peaceful/good land' (or gsar sde 'new district'), a town in Kangding, Garze.

b_dawu.first_mention_attestation: Dawu (rta'u, Daofu) has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE; it was part of the Hor States in the early modern period and established as Daowu/Daofu County in 1912–1913 CE.
b_dawu.etymology_analysis: Tibetan rta'u means 'colt', reportedly named because the valley terrain viewed from the surrounding mountains resembles a horse.

b_nyatsho.first_mention_attestation: Nyatsho Gompa (Lingque Monastery) in Dawu was founded in 1662 CE (first year of the Kangxi reign).
b_nyatsho.etymology_analysis: Nyatsho (Lingque Monastery, 灵雀寺) is one of the 13 Gelugpa monasteries in Kham, founded in 1662 CE.

b_rongzhag.first_mention_attestation: Rongzhag (rong brag, Danba) has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Danba County was established in 1912 CE.
b_rongzhag.etymology_analysis: Tibetan rong brag means 'valley cliffs' or 'agricultural gorge crags', describing the steep Gyalrong valley of Danba.

b_draggo.first_mention_attestation: Draggo (brag 'go, Luhuo) has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the Hor State of Draggo was founded in the 15th–16th century CE by Norbu, son of Namkha Gyaltsen.
b_draggo.etymology_analysis: Tibetan brag 'go means 'cliff head' or 'top of the rock', referring to the rocky promontory in Luhuo.

b_lhagang.first_mention_attestation: Lhagang (lha sgang, Tagong) is associated in later oral and written legends with Princess Wencheng's 641 CE journey, but Lhagang/Tagong Monastery was built in the Qing dynasty (17th century CE) with no contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_lhagang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan lha sgang is traditionally interpreted as 'place loved by the Bodhisattva' (or 'divine ridge').

b_gyezil.first_mention_attestation: Gyezil (Gyezur, brgyad zur, Jiulong) has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE; it formed part of the Chakla Kingdom by the early 18th century CE.
b_gyezil.etymology_analysis: Tibetan brgyad zur (Gyezur/Gyezil) means 'eight corners' or 'eight valleys', corresponding to Jiulong in Garze.

b_sertar.first_mention_attestation: Sertar (gser rta, Seda) was a nomadic pastoral region outside formal tusi administration until the 20th century CE, with Sertar County established in 1955 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_sertar.etymology_analysis: Tibetan gser rta means 'golden horse', named after a legend of finding a horse-shaped gold nugget in Sertang.

b_larung.first_mention_attestation: Larung Gar Buddhist Academy in Larung Valley, Sertar, was founded in 1980 CE by Khenpo Jigme Phuntsok (building on a late-19th-century hermitage of Dudjom Lingpa).
b_larung.etymology_analysis: Larung (Tibetan: བླ་རུང་) refers to the Larung Valley in Sertar County, Sichuan.

b_niba.first_mention_attestation: Niba (Nyinba, nyin pa) has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE; the historical Tibetan village of Niba in Amdo/Gannan has a documented ~200-year history dating to the Qing dynasty.
b_niba.etymology_analysis: Tibetan nyin pa (Niba) refers to dwellers on the sunny slope; placed in Sertar in-game though historically a town in Jone County.

b_jone.first_mention_attestation: Jone (co ne, Chone) is traditionally traced to Tibetan border troops remaining after the late 10th century CE, and the Jone Tusi kingdom was formally recognized by the Ming Yongle Emperor in 1404 CE.
b_jone.etymology_analysis: Tibetan co ne (Jone, Chinese: 卓尼) was the seat of the hereditary Jone Kingdom (Tusi) from 1404 to 1949 CE.

b_linten.first_mention_attestation: Lintan County (临潭县) was established in 607 CE (3rd year of Daye, Sui dynasty) under Lintao Commandery and continued under Tang dynasty Taozhou before being renamed Taozhou in later dynasties and restored as Lintan in 1913 CE.
b_linten.etymology_analysis: Chinese Lintan (临潭) means 'facing the deep pool', a relational locator compound attested since 607 CE.

b_hzo.first_mention_attestation: 1777 CE (Qing Qianlong 42nd year): construction of the nine-story Milarepa Tower at Gtsos dgon pa (Heicuo Monastery); Chinese transliteration 'Heicuo' (黑错) was changed to 'Hezuo' (合作) in 1956 CE.
b_hzo.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Amdo Tibetan toponym gtsos (pronounced Zö/Hzö), glossed in local Chinese gazetteers as 'place where antelopes appear'. Transcribed into Chinese as Heicuo (黑错) before 1956 CE, when it was renamed to the homophonous Hezuo (合作, 'cooperation').

b_maqu.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for the settlement/county; Maqu County was formally established in 1953 CE (named after the Yellow River hydronym Rma chu, attested in Old Tibetan Dunhuang documents c. 750 CE).

morphemes.translation: peacock / traditional name of the Yellow River

b_maqu.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Pinyin (ZWPY) rendering of Rma chu (རྨ་ཆུ), the Tibetan hydronym for the Yellow River, composed of rma (peacock / river name) + chu (river).

b_murje.first_mention_attestation: 1906 CE: founding of Xiqiaqiang Monastery in Muxihe (Tibetan: mur byeg, ZWPY: Murqê / Murje), Maqu County; modern township established in the 20th century.
b_murje.etymology_analysis: Romanization of Tibetan mur byeg (མུར་བྱེག, ZWPY: Murqê), rendered in Chinese as Muxihe (木西合). No pre-20th-century etymology or attestation is documented.

b_sangqu.first_mention_attestation: 1709 CE: founding of Labrang Monastery in the Sangchu (bsang chu) valley; the county was named Xiahe ('Xia River') in 1928 CE after the Daxia River. No <= 867 CE attestation exists for the Tibetan name Bsang chu.
b_sangqu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Bsang chu (བསང་ཆུ, 'Incense River'), the Tibetan name of the Daxia River (大夏河), corresponding to Chinese Xiahe (夏河).

historical_names.name: Baishi
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Western Han, 81 BCE) and Tang records (715 CE / 754 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Han established Baishi County in 81 BCE; Tang established Zhenxi (715 CE) and Tiancheng (754 CE) garrisons at Suogongchuan in modern Xiahe.

historical_names.name: Suogongchuan
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Western Han, 81 BCE) and Tang records (715 CE / 754 CE)
historical_names.notes: Western Han established Baishi County in 81 BCE; Tang established Zhenxi (715 CE) and Tiancheng (754 CE) garrisons at Suogongchuan in modern Xiahe.

b_luqu.first_mention_attestation: 1953 CE: establishment of the Luqu administrative committee (formally Luqu County in 1955 CE), named after the Tibetan name of the Tao River (klu chu). No <= 867 CE attestation exists for Klu chu.
b_luqu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Klu chu (ཀླུ་ཆུ, 'Nāga/Spring-water River'), the Tibetan hydronym for the Tao River (洮河).

historical_names.name: Qiangchuan
historical_names.source: Chinese dynastic histories (Former Liang, Sui, and Old Book of Tang, 4th–8th centuries CE)
historical_names.notes: Former Liang established Qiangchuan Protectorate; Sui established Taoyuan and Taoyang counties; early Tang established Xicangzhou before it fell to Tibet in 715 CE.

historical_names.name: Taoyuan
historical_names.source: Chinese dynastic histories (Former Liang, Sui, and Old Book of Tang, 4th–8th centuries CE)
historical_names.notes: Former Liang established Qiangchuan Protectorate; Sui established Taoyuan and Taoyang counties; early Tang established Xicangzhou before it fell to Tibet in 715 CE.

historical_names.name: Taoyang
historical_names.source: Chinese dynastic histories (Former Liang, Sui, and Old Book of Tang, 4th–8th centuries CE)
historical_names.notes: Former Liang established Qiangchuan Protectorate; Sui established Taoyuan and Taoyang counties; early Tang established Xicangzhou before it fell to Tibet in 715 CE.

historical_names.name: Xicangzhou
historical_names.source: Chinese dynastic histories (Former Liang, Sui, and Old Book of Tang, 4th–8th centuries CE)
historical_names.notes: Former Liang established Qiangchuan Protectorate; Sui established Taoyuan and Taoyang counties; early Tang established Xicangzhou before it fell to Tibet in 715 CE.

b_tewo.first_mention_attestation: c. 12th century CE: earliest Tibetan references to The bo (ཐེ་བོ) in Bonpo hagiographies of Skyang 'phags and Gtso 'phags; Diebu County was established in 1962 CE.
b_tewo.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan the bo (ཐེ་བོ, 'thumb'), traditionally explained by a local legend in which a mountain deity pressed a passage through the mountains with his thumb.

historical_names.name: Tazhong
historical_names.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms (263 CE)
historical_names.notes: Known as Tazhong (沓中) in the Han and Three Kingdoms periods, where Shu Han general Jiang Wei stationed troops in 263 CE.

b_zhugqu.first_mention_attestation: 1954 CE: Xigu County was reorganized as the Zhugqu (Zhouqu) Administrative Committee (county in 1955 CE), named after the Tibetan name of the Bailong River ('brug chu). No <= 867 CE attestation exists for 'Brug chu.
b_zhugqu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan 'Brug chu (འབྲུག་ཆུ, 'Dragon River'), the Tibetan hydronym for the Bailong River (白龙江).

historical_names.name: Qiangdao
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian / Book of Han (279 BCE) and Old Book of Tang (618–627 CE)
historical_names.notes: Qin established Qiangdao in 279 BCE; Tang established Dangzhou and Huaidao County in the 7th century CE.

historical_names.name: Dangzhou
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian / Book of Han (279 BCE) and Old Book of Tang (618–627 CE)
historical_names.notes: Qin established Qiangdao in 279 BCE; Tang established Dangzhou and Huaidao County in the 7th century CE.

historical_names.name: Huaidao
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian / Book of Han (279 BCE) and Old Book of Tang (618–627 CE)
historical_names.notes: Qin established Qiangdao in 279 BCE; Tang established Dangzhou and Huaidao County in the 7th century CE.

b_seretang.first_mention_attestation: 1955 CE: establishment of Banma County with its seat at Sêlêtang / Sailaitang (赛来塘镇). No <= 867 CE attestation exists.
b_seretang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan toponym Sêlêtang (赛来塘), glossed in Chinese toponymic sources as 'golden plain/meadow' (from Tibetan gser 'gold' + thang 'plain').

b_gyumai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; modern town of Gyümai (རྒྱུ་སྨད, Chinese: Jimai 吉迈) serves as the seat of Darlag County (established 1952 CE) and contains a directional 'lower' (smad) morpheme.
b_gyumai.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Rgyu smad (རྒྱུ་སྨད), a directional/elevation compound meaning 'Lower Gyu' (smad = 'lower').

b_jigzhi.first_mention_attestation: 1955 CE: establishment of Jigzhi County (久治县, Tibetan: gcig sgril rdzong).
b_jigzhi.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan gcig sgril (གཅིག་སྒྲིལ, 'unity/unification'), a 1950s administrative name adopted upon county establishment.

b_madoi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; Madoi County (རྨ་སྟོད, Rma stod) was established in 1957 CE and is a directional/elevation compound ('Upper Rma [Yellow River]').
b_madoi.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Rma stod (རྨ་སྟོད), a directional/elevation compound meaning 'Upper Rma' (i.e., headwaters/upper reaches of the Yellow River).

b_dzogenrabar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; in-game barony in Madoi County mapped in the repository to Donggei (Lake Donggi Cona).
b_dzogenrabar.etymology_analysis: Unattested Tibetan-style toponym (possibly a compound ending in rab 'bar 'blazing/flourishing'); no verified historical or linguistic etymology is documented.

b_machu.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for the settlement; named after the Yellow River hydronym Rma chu (attested in Old Tibetan Dunhuang documents c. 750 CE), located in Madoi County (established 1957 CE).

morphemes.translation: peacock / traditional name of the Yellow River

b_machu.etymology_analysis: Standard/Wylie-based transcription of Tibetan Rma chu (རྨ་ཆུ), the Tibetan hydronym for the Yellow River, composed of rma (river name/peacock) + chu (river).

b_maqen.first_mention_attestation: 1954 CE: establishment of Maqên County (玛沁县), named after the sacred mountain Anyê Maqên (ཨ་མྱེས་རྨ་ཆེན, Rma chen); written attestations of Rma chen in Bon/Gesar literature postdate 867 CE.
b_maqen.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Rma chen (རྨ་ཆེན, 'Great Rma / Highest Mountain of the Yellow River Source'), named after the Amnye Machen massif.

b_gade.first_mention_attestation: 1954 CE: establishment of Gadê County (甘德县, Tibetan: dga' bde rdzong) in Golog Prefecture.
b_gade.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan dga' bde (དགའ་བདེ), meaning 'joy, peace, and happiness'.

b_barkam.first_mention_attestation: 1953 CE: establishment of the Barkam (Ma'erkang) Office (county in 1955 CE), named after a local monastery ('bar khams). No <= 867 CE written attestation exists for 'Bar khams.
b_barkam.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan 'bar khams (འབར་ཁམས), literally 'place of strong fire / blazing incense', by extension 'place of prosperity', originally referring to a local monastery.

historical_names.name: Wenshan Commandery
historical_names.source: Book of Han (established 111 BCE under Emperor Wu of Han)
historical_names.notes: Han Wenshan Commandery (and Tang/Song Jimi prefectures) administered the upper Min River / Gyalrong region prior to the Ming-Qing Gyalrong Tusi era.

b_rongbur.first_mention_attestation: Mid-20th century CE: modern administrative township of Ribu (日部乡, Tibetan: rdzong 'bur) in Barkam, Sichuan. No <= 867 CE attestation exists.
b_rongbur.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan rdzong 'bur (རྫོང་འབུར, 'protruding fortress/mound'), rendered in Chinese as Ribu (日部) and in-game as Rongbur.

b_zamtang.first_mention_attestation: 1958 CE: establishment of Zamthang / Rangtang County (壤塘县), named after a local village whose hill resembled Jambhala (dzam bha la).
b_zamtang.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan 'Dzam thang (འཛམ་ཐང), shortened from Dzam bha la thang ('Plain of Jambhala'), named after a local village next to a hill shaped like the wealth deity Jambhala.

b_soxiq.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; in-game county capital of c_ngawa mapped in the repository to Ngawa.
b_soxiq.etymology_analysis: Unattested Tibetan-style toponym; no verified historical attestation or linguistic etymology is documented.

b_ngawa.first_mention_attestation: 1108 CE: founding of Nangzhig Monastery in rNga ba (at the confluence of the lDing chu and rNga chu rivers); later attested in Ming Yongle-era 'Three Aba' (上中下阿坝) and Ngawa County (1954 CE).
b_ngawa.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan rNga ba (རྔ་བ, pronounced Ngawa in Amdo Tibetan and transcribed as Aba 阿坝 in Chinese), referring to the inhabitants of the rNga khog valley.

historical_names.name: Quanzhou Dudufu
historical_names.source: Tang Dynasty administrative records (7th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Early Tang Jiannan Circuit administered the area under Quanzhou Dudufu (one of 168 Jimi prefectures) before Tibetan expansion in 638 CE.

b_khyungchu.first_mention_attestation: 1960 CE: establishment of Hongyuan County with its seat at Kyungqu / Khyungchu (邛溪镇).
b_khyungchu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Khyung mchu (ཁྱུང་མཆུ, 'Garuda's Beak' or 'Garuda River'), the Tibetan name for the county seat of Hongyuan County (Gakog).

b_quqen.first_mention_attestation: c. 1700–1747 CE: Greater Jinchuan (Tibetan Chiefdom of Chuchen / Chu chen) attested in Qing Jinchuan campaign records; Jinchuan County renamed in 1960 CE.
b_quqen.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Chu chen (ཆུ་ཆེན, ZWPY: Quqên, 'Great River'), referring to the upper Dadu (Great Jinchuan) River.

historical_names.name: Jinchuan Jimi Prefecture
historical_names.source: Tang Dynasty administrative records (7th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Tang established Jinchuan Jimi Prefecture in the 7th century CE before Tibetan occupation of the Bailan (Gyalrong) region.

historical_names.name: Bailan
historical_names.source: Tang Dynasty administrative records (7th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Tang established Jinchuan Jimi Prefecture in the 7th century CE before Tibetan occupation of the Bailan (Gyalrong) region.

b_kharsa.first_mention_attestation: Mid-20th century CE: modern Kasa Township (卡撒乡, Tibetan: mkhar sa) in Jinchuan County, Sichuan. No <= 867 CE attestation exists.
b_kharsa.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan mkhar sa (མཁར་ས, 'fortress place/land'), rendered in Chinese as Kasa (卡撒).

b_zainlha.first_mention_attestation: 1747 CE: Lesser Jinchuan (Gyalrong Tibetan Chiefdom of Tsanlha / Btsan lha) documented in the Qing Jinchuan campaigns (1747–1776 CE); renamed Xiaojin County in 1953 CE.
b_zainlha.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Btsan lha (བཙན་ལྷ, ZWPY: Zänlha / Zainlha), meaning 'fierce deity' (referring to a local Bon/mountain deity).

b_trashingling.first_mention_attestation: Mid-20th century CE: modern Zhaxiling / Zagunao Town (杂谷脑镇, Tibetan: bkra shis gling), seat of Li County, Sichuan. No <= 867 CE attestation exists.
b_trashingling.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Bkra shis gling (བཀྲ་ཤིས་གླིང, 'Auspicious Land/Sanctuary'), corresponding to Chinese Zhaxiling / Zagunao.

b_sungqu.first_mention_attestation: Ming/Qing period (post-867 CE): Tibetan name Zung chu (ཟུང་ཆུ, ZWPY: Sungqu) for Songpan; the Chinese name Songzhou (松州) is attested earlier in 618 CE.

morphemes.translation: pair, junction (or phonetic adaptation of Songzhou)

b_sungqu.etymology_analysis: Tibetan name Zung chu (ཟུང་ཆུ, ZWPY: Sungqu) for Songpan County and its river.

historical_names.name: Jiandi Dao
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian (316 BCE) and Old Book of Tang (618 CE, 638 CE)
historical_names.notes: Qin established Jiandi Dao in 316 BCE; Western Wei established Gansong County; Tang established Songzhou in 618 CE (site of the 638 CE Tibetan attack under Songtsen Gampo).

historical_names.name: Gansong
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian (316 BCE) and Old Book of Tang (618 CE, 638 CE)
historical_names.notes: Qin established Jiandi Dao in 316 BCE; Western Wei established Gansong County; Tang established Songzhou in 618 CE (site of the 638 CE Tibetan attack under Songtsen Gampo).

historical_names.name: Songzhou
historical_names.source: Records of the Grand Historian (316 BCE) and Old Book of Tang (618 CE, 638 CE)
historical_names.notes: Qin established Jiandi Dao in 316 BCE; Western Wei established Gansong County; Tang established Songzhou in 618 CE (site of the 638 CE Tibetan attack under Songtsen Gampo).

b_choqu.first_mention_attestation: Early 18th century CE (Qing / Ming-Qing Tusi period): Gyalrong polity of Trochu (Tibetan: khro chu); Heishui County was established in 1952–1954 CE.
b_choqu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Khro chu (ཁྲོ་ཆུ, ZWPY: Choqu), the Tibetan hydronym for the Heishui River ('Black Water River' in Chinese).

b_zoige.first_mention_attestation: 1953 CE: establishment of the Zoigê-Baozuo Administrative Committee (separated from Songpan as Zoigê County in 1956 CE). No <= 867 CE attestation exists.
b_zoige.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Mdzod dge (མཛོད་དགེ, ZWPY: Zoigê, Chinese: Ruo'ergai 若尔盖), literally 'treasury of virtue' (and the name of a local Tibetan tribe).

b_yunglro.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; in-game barony in Zoigê mapped in the repository to Jiuzhaigou (formerly Nanping County).
b_yunglro.etymology_analysis: Unattested Tibetan-style toponym; no verified historical attestation or linguistic etymology is documented.

b_mangra.first_mention_attestation: 1953 CE: establishment of Guinan County (Tibetan: mang ra rdzong, containing Mangra Township). No <= 867 CE attestation exists.
b_mangra.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Mang ra (མང་ར), the Tibetan name for Mangra Township and Guinan County.

b_gabasumdo.first_mention_attestation: 1953 CE: Tongde County seat relocated to Gabasumdo (尕巴松多镇). No <= 867 CE attestation exists.
b_gabasumdo.etymology_analysis: From Amdo Tibetan Gabasumdo (尕巴松多), containing sum mdo ('three-way river/valley confluence').

historical_names.name: Chishui
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (609 CE) and Tang records (663 CE)
historical_names.notes: Sui Dynasty placed the area under Chishui County (609 CE); Tang established the Dushan Military Garrison after 663 CE.

historical_names.name: Dushan Garrison
historical_names.source: Book of Sui (609 CE) and Tang records (663 CE)
historical_names.notes: Sui Dynasty placed the area under Chishui County (609 CE); Tang established the Dushan Military Garrison after 663 CE.

b_rebgong.first_mention_attestation: 1342 CE: establishment of the Rongwo Nangso polity of Rebgong (reb kong) by Dodé Bum's family; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists for Rebgong.
b_rebgong.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Reb gong / Reb kong (རེབ་གོང / རེབ་ཀོང), variously explained in Tibetan sources as 'above Repsa' or 'Kongpo settlers', and popularly glossed as 'Golden Valley where dreams come true'.

b_jainca.first_mention_attestation: 1953 CE: establishment of Jainca County (尖扎县, Tibetan: gcan tsha rdzong), named after the local Jainca Tibetan tribe/plain; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_jainca.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Gcan tsha (གཅན་ཚ), interpreted in Tibetan sources as 'dangerous place with wild beasts' or linked to the Tsha rigs clan.

b_triga.first_mention_attestation: 1271 CE: establishment of Guidezhou (贵德州); local Tibetan histories also record the Trika (khri ka) Yülha temple's founding in 1179–1368 CE. Although oral legend links Khri ka to 9th-century King Tri Ralpachan, no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

morphemes.translation: throne, ten thousand (or royal title Tri)

b_triga.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Khri ka / Khri ga (ཁྲི་ཀ), the Tibetan name for Guide County, traditionally linked to King Tri Ralpachan.

historical_names.name: Heguan
historical_names.source: Book of Han (Western Han Dynasty)
historical_names.notes: Situated within Western Han Heguan County (河关县) prior to the Yuan establishment of Guidezhou in 1271 CE.

b_zekog.first_mention_attestation: 1953 CE: establishment of Zêkog County (泽库县, Tibetan: rtse khog rdzong), named after the Zequ River valley. No <= 867 CE attestation exists.
b_zekog.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Rtse khog (རྩེ་ཁོག, 'highland valley'), named after the Zequ (རྩེ་ཆུ) river valley.

b_yegainnyin.first_mention_attestation: 1954 CE: establishment of the Henan Mongol Autonomous Region (county in 1955/1964 CE) with its seat at Yêgainnyin (优干宁镇). No <= 867 CE attestation exists.
b_yegainnyin.etymology_analysis: Modern Amdo Tibetan/Chinese administrative town name (Yêgainnyin / Youganning 优干宁), seat of Henan Mongol Autonomous County.

b_batang.first_mention_attestation: Yuan Dynasty (late 13th century CE): establishment of the Batang Pacification Commission (巴塘招讨司). No <= 867 CE written attestation exists for 'Ba' thang / Batang.
b_batang.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan 'Ba' thang (འབའ་ཐང), meaning 'vast plain where sheep can be heard bleating everywhere'.

historical_names.name: Bailang
historical_names.source: Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu, Bailang Songs, c. 100 CE)
historical_names.notes: Inhabited by the Bailang Qiang in the Eastern Han period (distinct from the Sui–Tang Bailan / 白兰 polity on the northeastern Tibetan Plateau, audited on b_quqen).

b_dewu.first_mention_attestation: Mid-20th century CE: modern Dewu Town (地巫镇) in Batang County, Garzê, Sichuan. No <= 867 CE attestation exists.
b_dewu.etymology_analysis: Local Kham Tibetan toponym in Batang County rendered in Chinese as Dewu (地巫); no pre-modern etymology is documented.

b_qagcheng.first_mention_attestation: 1906 CE: Qing gaitu guiliu reorganization of Xiangcheng (Tibetan: phyag phreng, ZWPY: Qagchêng) as Dingxiang County (定乡县), formerly under the Litang Tusi.
b_qagcheng.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Phyag phreng (ཕྱག་ཕྲེང, ZWPY: Qagchêng), meaning 'prayer beads in hand', transliterated into Chinese as Xiangcheng (乡城).

b_deqen.first_mention_attestation: 17th century CE: renamed Dêqên (bde chen, 'supreme bliss') by the Fifth Dalai Lama (formerly Jol / Atunzi 阿墩子); Deqin County Bureau established 1935 CE.
b_deqen.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Bde chen (བདེ་ཆེན, 'great bliss / supreme peace'), named after the Deqen Ling monastery in the 17th century CE.

b_balung.first_mention_attestation: Early 18th century CE: Balung ('ba' lung) attested as a Karma Kagyu monastic center in Situ Panchen's travel records; modern Tibetan name of Weixi Lisu Autonomous County.
b_balung.etymology_analysis: Tibetan name 'Ba' lung (འབའ་ལུང, ZWPY: Balung) for Weixi Lisu Autonomous County, containing lung ('valley').

historical_names.name: Shenchuan Dudufu / Tieqiao
historical_names.source: Chinese Tang/Nanzhao records (794 CE) and Yu Qingyuan's Weixi Jianwenji
historical_names.notes: Early Tibetan Empire established Tieqiao Jiedushi / Shenchuan Dudufu (with its West City at Qizong Village in Weixi), captured by Nanzhao in 794 CE.

b_gyaitang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; the Tibetan name Gyalthang (rgyal thang) is attested in later Ming-Qing records (e.g., Jiantang tusi) and the 17th-century foundation of Sumtsenling Monastery (1674–1679 CE).
b_gyaitang.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan rgyal thang ('royal plain' or 'victorious plain'), referring to the high-altitude basin in northwestern Yunnan (modern Shangri-La City, formerly Zhongdian).

b_takchongrong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; appears only as a local Kham sub-barony toponym in modern administrative and game-map compilations.
b_takchongrong.etymology_analysis: A Tibetan compound toponym likely corresponding to stag mchog rong ('supreme tiger gorge/valley') or rtag chong rong, designating a local valley holding in the Gyaitang area.

b_derong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; formerly known as Delong under the Batang tusi, and formally established as Derong County in 1913 CE during the Republic of China.
b_derong.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan sde rong, meaning 'district of canyons' or 'canyon valley', referring to the deep river gorges of southwestern Sichuan.

b_markam.first_mention_attestation: Although Tibetan Empire-era rock carvings (7th–9th centuries CE) and Tang-era salt wells exist in the area, the specific regional toponym Markam (smar khams) is not attested in written sources by 867 CE and belongs to the post-imperial 'Six Ranges' (sgang drug) geographic framework.
b_markam.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan smar khams (often in smar khams sgang, one of the Six Ranges of Kham), designating the southeastern borderland of Kham.

b_jangpa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; documented as Jangpa Miri ('jang pa mi ri) in modern Tibetan gazetteers and THL place-name records for Markam County.
b_jangpa.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan 'jang pa (referring to the Jang/Naxi people or borderland inhabitants in Markam, as in the township Jangpa Miri).

b_baxoi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the area lay within the Tibetan Empire (7th–9th centuries CE) and Ming-era Mo'erkan tusi, while the specific name Pasho/Baxoi (dpa' shod) is first attested with the establishment of the Pasho Larang in 1694 CE.
b_baxoi.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan dpa' shod ('lower valley of the brave/heroes'), romanized as Pasho or Baxoi.

b_rawu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; the lakeside settlement and 17th-century Gelugpa monastery at Rawu (Ranwu) are documented only in post-imperial and modern sources.
b_rawu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ra 'og (THL: Raok; also Rawu/Ranwu), associated with the nearby Rakwa Tso (Rawu Lake) in Baxoi County.

b_bome.first_mention_attestation: The modern administrative name Bome (spo mes) was adopted when Bomê County was formed in 1960 CE from Dzongdor, Boqu, and Yigong; the region itself was known since the Tibetan Empire (7th–9th centuries CE) as Powo (spo bo) or Poyul (spo yul).
b_bome.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan spo mes (Bomê), a modern administrative form derived from the ancient regional choronym spo bo (Powo) / spo yul (Poyul).

historical_names.name: Powo
historical_names.source: Tibetan Empire-era histories and traditional Yarlung chronicles (e.g., semi-autonomous Powo region since the Tubo era)
historical_names.notes: Powo (spo bo) and Poyul (spo yul) were the historical names of the region from the 7th–9th century Tibetan Empire onward.

historical_names.name: Poyul
historical_names.source: Tibetan Empire-era histories and traditional Yarlung chronicles (e.g., semi-autonomous Powo region since the Tubo era)
historical_names.notes: Powo (spo bo) and Poyul (spo yul) were the historical names of the region from the 7th–9th century Tibetan Empire onward.

b_zhamog.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Tramog / Zhamog (spra rmog) is attested in later records as the seat of Bomê County.
b_zhamog.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan spra rmog (THL: Tramok; Chinese/pinyin Zhamog/Zhamo), the town serving as the administrative seat of Bomê County.

b_kangyu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; documented as a modern township (khang yul) in Bomê County.
b_kangyu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan khang yul (THL: Khangyül; Tibetan Pinyin: Kangyu), meaning 'land of houses' or 'village of dwellings', a township in Bomê County.

b_qundo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; documented only as a modern town (Qundo / Qingduo) in Bomê County.
b_qundo.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Pinyin Qundo (Chinese: Qingduo), a town in Bomê County corresponding to a Tibetan toponym ending in -mdo ('confluence / valley').

b_zogang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Zogang (mdzod sgang) is documented in later Tibetan and modern Chamdo county records.
b_zogang.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan mdzod sgang ('treasury ridge' or 'dzo-hybrid yak ridge'), a county in Chamdo, eastern Tibet.

b_kagong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; documented only as a modern village/township toponym (Kagong / Khargang) in eastern Tibet.
b_kagong.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan mkhar sgang ('fort ridge'), rendered in Chinese/Tibetan Pinyin as Kagong.

b_dege.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; according to Tibetan histories, the area was named Dege (sde dge) around 1446 CE when Tangtong Gyelpo founded Lhündrupteng Monastery for the Gar clan, and the Kingdom of Derge rose to prominence in the 1630s CE.
b_dege.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan sde dge ('land of mercy/virtue'), traditionally explained as a contraction of phun tshogs sde bzhi ('four abundances') and dge ba bcu ('ten virtues').

b_palpung.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Palpung Monastery originated in the 12th century CE and the extant monastic seat in Derge was founded in 1727 CE by the 8th Tai Situpa, Situ Panchen.
b_palpung.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan dpal spungs ('glorious heap' or 'glorious union of study and practice'), the Karma Kagyu monastic seat in Kham.

b_dzogchen.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Dzogchen Monastery in northern Derge was founded in 1684 CE by Pema Rigdzin, the 1st Dzogchen Rinpoche.
b_dzogchen.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan rdzogs chen ('Great Perfection'), named after the highest Nyingma meditative tradition.

b_garze.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Garze (Kardze) Monastery was founded in 1662 CE by Hor Chöjé Ngawang Phuntsok, giving its name to the surrounding Hor state and modern county.
b_garze.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan dkar mdzes ('white and beautiful/fair'), romanized as Garzê or Kardze (Chinese: Ganzi).

b_axu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Axu (a phyug) is documented in later Kham/Derge local records and Gesar epic folklore.
b_axu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan a phyug (Tibetan Pinyin: Axu), a town and grassland in northeastern Dêgê County.

b_pelyul.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Palyul (Pelyul) Monastery was founded in 1665 CE by Rigzin Kunzang Sherab in Baiyü County.
b_pelyul.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan dpal yul ('auspicious/glorious land'), one of the Six Mother Monasteries of the Nyingma school and the Tibetan name of Baiyü County.

b_katok.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Kathok Monastery was founded in 1159 CE by Katok Dampa Deshek, making it the oldest Nyingma mother monastery in Kham.
b_katok.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan kaH thog ('above the letter Ka'), referring to a rock naturally marked with the Tibetan letter Ka at the monastery site.

b_manigango.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Manigango (ma ni sgang mgo) appears in later Derge/Sichuan-Tibet caravan route records.
b_manigango.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ma ni sgang mgo ('head of the mani-stone ridge'), a crossroads town in Dêgê County.

b_bolo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Bolo ('bo lo) is documented in later records as the seat of Gonjo County, while Gonjo itself is attested from the 13th century CE (1270 CE).
b_bolo.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan 'bo lo (Tibetan Pinyin: Bolo; Chinese: Moluo), the administrative seat of Gonjo County in Chamdo.

b_bumgye.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; documented only as a modern township ('bum skyes) in Gonjo County.
b_bumgye.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan 'bum skyes (THL: Bumkyé; Tibetan Pinyin: Bumgyê), a township in Gonjo County, Chamdo.

b_lhatok.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Lhatok (lha thog) is documented as one of the five major post-imperial kingdoms of Kham (13th–19th centuries CE).
b_lhatok.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan lha thog ('summit/roof of the deities'), a historical Kham polity located in eastern Chamdo.

b_jomda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Jomda ('jo mda') is documented in later Derge/Chamdo records.
b_jomda.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan 'jo mda' ('lower end/mouth of the Jo valley'), a county in Chamdo.

b_derdoin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Derdoin (Dêrdoin) is documented only as a modern mountain/monastic locality in Jomda County, Chamdo.
b_derdoin.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Pinyin Derdoin (Dêrdoin), a monastic and mountain locality in Jomda County, Chamdo.

b_yendum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Yendum (dbyen 'dum) is documented in modern records as the seat of Zhag'yab (Dagyab) County.
b_yendum.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan dbyen 'dum ('reconciliation of discord'), the town serving as the seat of Zhag'yab County in Chamdo.

b_rongzhub.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; documented only as a modern township (Rongzhub / Rongzhou) in Zhag'yab County.
b_rongzhub.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Pinyin Rongzhub (Chinese: Rongzhou), a township in Zhag'yab County, Chamdo.

b_ariksar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; documented only as a modern settlement/township (Ariksar) in Sêrxü County.
b_ariksar.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan a rig gsar ('New Arik'), a settlement in Sêrxü County, Garzê Prefecture.

b_tromsa_genma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; appears only in modern local/game-map compilations for the Sêrxü/Lingtsang area.
b_tromsa_genma.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan khrom sa rgan ma ('old marketplace/assembly site'), a sub-barony holding in the Ariksar/Lingtsang area.

b_lingtsang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Lingtsang (gling tshang) emerged in the mid-13th century CE (c. 1253–1270 CE) as a Sakya-Mongol polity when Chögyel Pakpa appointed the Lingtsang head as great chief of Domé.
b_lingtsang.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan gling tshang ('House/Lineage of Ling'), one of the five major kingdoms of Kham.

b_serxu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Sershul Monastery, the religious center of Sêrxü (ser shul), was founded in 1701 CE.
b_serxu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ser shul (romanized as Sêrxü or Sershul; Chinese: Shiqu), a county and monastery in northern Garzê Prefecture.

b_lenggu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Lenggu Monastery (gnas sgo dgon) at the foot of Mount Ge'nyen was originally built in 1164 CE by the 1st Karmapa, Düsum Khyenpa.
b_lenggu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan gnas sgo ('sacred gate'), rendered in Chinese Pinyin as Lenggu (Lenggu Monastery).

b_dabba_tibet.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Dabba ('dab pa) is the traditional Tibetan name for Daocheng County (renamed Daocheng in 1911 CE).
b_dabba_tibet.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan 'dab pa (Dabba/Dapba), referring to the mountain-flanked valley of Daocheng County in Garzê Prefecture.

b_muli.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Muli (smi li) entered Tibetan imperial/post-imperial records after 1253 CE and became a Qing tusi kingdom in 1729 CE.
b_muli.etymology_analysis: From Written Tibetan smi li (or mu li), romanized as Muli, a historical Tibetan monastic kingdom in southwestern Sichuan.

b_litang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporaneous written sources by 867 CE (later sources retroactively include it in Songtsen Gampo's 7th-century empire); first documented administratively in 1278 CE when the Yuan Dynasty organized Litang as a circuit (lu).
b_litang.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan li thang ('copper-colored plain' or 'mirror-flat plain'), referring to the high-altitude Maoya/Litang plateau in Kham.

b_nyagqu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Nyagqu / Nyagchukha (nyag chu kha) is documented in later Kham and Qing/Republican records as the ferry crossing on the Yalong River.
b_nyagqu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan nyag chu (Yalong River; also nyag chu kha, 'mouth/bank of the Nyag River'), romanized as Nyagqu (Chinese: Yajiang).

b_nyagrong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE (though Imperial-era Nyingma/Bon presence is noted in later histories); first dated attestation is 1253 CE under the Chakdü (lcags mdud) chieftaincy granted by Kublai Khan.
b_nyagrong.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan nyag rong ('valley of the Nyag [Yalong] River'), modern Xinlong County in Garzê Prefecture.

b_jalhaxi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; documented only as a modern township (Jialaxi / rGyarwagshis) in Xinlong (Nyagrong) County.
b_jalhaxi.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Pinyin Jalhaxi (Chinese: Jialaxi), a township in Xinlong (Nyagrong) County, Sichuan.

b_gyegumdo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; Gyegumdo (skye dgu mdo) developed as a Tibetan trade mart under the Nangchen kingdom (founded 13th–14th centuries CE).
b_gyegumdo.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan skye dgu mdo ('confluence of all beings'), romanized as Gyêgumdo or Jyekundo (modern Yushu/Gyêgu, Qinghai).

b_longbaoco.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources by 867 CE; documented only in modern geographical and nature-reserve records for Yushu, Qinghai.
b_longbaoco.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Chinese-Tibetan / Tibetan Pinyin Longbaoco (Longbao Lake, with Tibetan mtsho 'lake'), a high-altitude wetland lake near Yushu in Qinghai.

b_nangqen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in connection with the founding of the Kingdom of Nangchen (nang chen rgyal po) in 1175 CE by Wa Alu.
