b_nangqen.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ནང་ཆེན (nang chen, 'great inner [palace/minister]'), derived from the title of the ruling Nangchen king/lineage (nang chen rgyal po) that emerged in the late 12th–13th century CE.

b_nyangla.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern township in Nangqen County, Qinghai.
b_nyangla.etymology_analysis: Modern Tibetan toponym (rendered in Chinese as 娘拉 Niangla and in Tibetan administrative orthography as ཉག་ར nyag ra) in Nangqen County, Yushu Prefecture.

b_gongbo.first_mention_attestation: Documented in the Old Tibetan Kongpo Inscription (rKong-po inscription, c. 799–815 CE) from the reign of Emperor Sadnalegs, and in the Old Tibetan Chronicle.
b_gongbo.etymology_analysis: From Old Tibetan རྐོང་པོ (rKong-po, modern ཀོང་པོ Kong-po / Gongbo), the historic southeastern Tibetan polity and region attested in imperial-era epigraphy (c. 799–815 CE).

b_nyang.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE specifically for this Kongpo settlement or river name (though the Nyang / Myang clan and principality appear in Old Tibetan Dunhuang manuscripts alongside Kongpo); modern Nyang River (Nyang-chu) in Nyingchi.
b_nyang.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཉང (nyang), referring to the Nyang River (ཉང་ཆུ nyang chu) and the local Nyang clan in Kongpo/Nyingchi.

b_pagsum.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern Pagsum Lake (Dragsum Tsho) in Gongbo'gyamda County.
b_pagsum.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan བྲག་གསུམ (brag gsum, 'three rocks', full name brag gsum mtsho 'Three Rocks Lake'), referring to the alpine lake in Gongbo'gyamda County.

b_nyingchi.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for the specific name Nyingchi; the region was historically part of Kongpo before Nyingchi Prefecture was established in 1960 CE.
b_nyingchi.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཉིང་ཁྲི (nying khri), a variant of ཉང་ཁྲི (nyang khri), combining the Nyang and Khri clan/river names near the lower Nyang River.

historical_names.name: Kongpo
historical_names.source: Old Tibetan Kongpo Inscription (rKong-po inscription, c. 799–815 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Nyingchi region was historically part of Kongpo (rKong-po, attested c. 799–815 CE; audited separately as b_gongbo) before Nyingchi Prefecture was established in 1960 CE.

b_burqug.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE; Buchu Monastery (Bu-chu) is traditionally attributed to Songtsen Gampo (7th century CE) in post-imperial 11th–12th century Tibetan chronicles.
b_burqug.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan བུ་ཆུ (bu chu, Chinese/Pinyin transcription Burqug / Bujiu), referring to the tributary stream and ancient Buchu Monastery south of Bayi in Nyingchi.

b_lunang.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; formally established as a township in 1988 CE.
b_lunang.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཀླུ་ནང (klu nang, 'Valley of the Nāgas/Dragons'), referring to the forested alpine valley east of Nyingchi.

b_yiong.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Yi'ong (Yigong) dzong was consolidated into Bomê County in 1960 CE.
b_yiong.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཡིད་འོང (yid 'ong, 'delightful / charming'), naming the Yi'ong Tsangpo river and valley in Bomê County.

b_banbar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Banbar County in Chamdo, eastern Tibet.
b_banbar.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan དཔལ་འབར (dpal 'bar, 'blazing glory'), an auspicious Tibetan toponym for Banbar County in Chamdo.

b_jaggang.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Tibetan toponym (lCags-sgang) used as a sub-barony in Banbar.
b_jaggang.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ལྕགས་སྒང (lcags sgang, 'iron ridge'), a topographic settlement name.

b_lhorong.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; directional compound ('south valley') for Lhorong County in Chamdo.
b_lhorong.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ལྷོ་རོང (lho rong, 'south valley' or 'southern gorge'), a directional compound describing the valley along the Nu (Salween) River.

b_baqen.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Baqên County in Nagqu.
b_baqen.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan སྦྲ་ཆེན (sbra chen, 'great yak-hair tent'), referring to a nomadic pastoral encampment in northeastern Tibet.

b_lhaxi.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern town (Lhaxi) in Baqên County, Nagqu.
b_lhaxi.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ལྷ་རི་ལྷ་ཤིང / ལྷ་ཞི (lha shing / lha zhi, Chinese 拉西 Lāxī), a settlement in Baqên County.

b_arxog.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern township (Arxog) in Baqên County, Nagqu.
b_arxog.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཨར་ཤོག (ar shog, Chinese 阿秀 Āxiù), a township in Baqên County.

b_dengqen.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Dêngqên County in Chamdo.
b_dengqen.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan སྟེང་ཆེན (steng chen, 'great upper terrace'), a directional/elevational compound for Dêngqên County.

b_qizhu.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern town (Chidu / Qizhu) in Dêngqên County, Chamdo.
b_qizhu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཁྲི་འདུ (khri 'du, Chinese 尺牍 Chǐdú, traditionally glossed as 'ten thousand'), a historic dzong and modern town in Dêngqên County.

b_damdoi.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; directional/elevational compound ('upper Dam') for Damdoi Township in Dêngqên County.
b_damdoi.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan གཏམ་སྟོད (gtam stod, 'upper Dam'), an elevational subdivision compound in Dêngqên County.

b_qamdo.first_mention_attestation: Visited by Je Tsongkhapa in 1373 CE; Galden Jampaling Monastery was subsequently constructed at Chamdo between 1436 and 1444 CE.
b_qamdo.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཆབ་མདོ (chab mdo, 'confluence of two rivers'), referring to the junction of the Za Qu and Ngom Qu rivers that form the Mekong (Lancang).

b_karub.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for the Tibetan name mKhar-ro; the nearby Karub archaeological site dates to the Neolithic (c. 3300–2000 BCE).
b_karub.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan མཁར་རོ (mkhar ro, 'ruined fort'), the village and district in Chamdo after which the Karub Neolithic culture is named.

b_riwoqe.first_mention_attestation: First attested with the founding of Riwoche Monastery (Ri-bo-che) in 1276 CE by Sangye Ön.
b_riwoqe.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan རི་བོ་ཆེ (ri bo che, 'great mountain'), naming the county and major Taklung Kagyu monastery founded in 1276 CE.

b_yiqen.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern township (Yiqên) in Chamdo Prefecture.
b_yiqen.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཡིད་ཆེན (yid chen, 'great mind/faith'), a township name in Chamdo Prefecture.

b_sog.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Sog County (Sog-rdzong) on the Sogchu River in Nagqu.
b_sog.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan སོག (sog), naming Sog County along the Sogchu River in eastern Nagqu.

b_riwar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern township (Riwar) in Sog County, Nagqu.
b_riwar.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan རི་དབར (ri dbar, 'between mountains'), a topographic locator compound in Sog County.

b_biru.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Biru County in Nagqu (local Samda Bon Monastery founded 1465 CE).
b_biru.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan འབྲི་རུ ('bri ru, 'female yak [herd]'), naming Biru County in Nagqu.

b_xamqu.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; directional/elevational compound ('lower river') for Xamqu Town in Biru County.
b_xamqu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan གཤམ་ཆུ (gsham chu, 'lower river'), an elevational/directional hydronymic compound in Biru County.

b_bumthang.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally associated with 7th-century Jampa Lhakhang and 8th-century Padmasambhava/Sindhu Raja (746 CE), but only attested in post-imperial Tibetan and Bhutanese chronicles from the 12th century CE onward; no contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_bumthang.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan/Dzongkha བུམ་ཐང (bum thang, 'plain of the vase' or 'plain of spirits'), the central Bhutanese valley and historical kingdom.

b_lhuentse.first_mention_attestation: First attested with the establishment of a temple/meditation seat in 1543 CE by Khedrup Kuenga Wangpo (son of Pema Lingpa), followed by Lhuentse Dzong in 1654 CE.
b_lhuentse.etymology_analysis: From Dzongkha/Tibetan ལྷུན་རྩེ (lhun rtse, 'lofty/spontaneous peak'), referring to the ridge-top dzong in northeastern Bhutan.

b_kurtoed.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; directional/elevational compound ('upper Kuri [Chhu]') for the historical Kurtoed region in Lhuentse.
b_kurtoed.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan/Dzongkha སྐུར་སྟོད (skur stod, 'upper Kuri Chhu'), an elevational subdivision of the Kuri Chhu valley.

b_kurmaed.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; directional/elevational compound ('lower Kuri [Chhu]') for the historical Kurmaed province in eastern Bhutan.
b_kurmaed.etymology_analysis: From Classical Tibetan/Dzongkha སྐུར་སྨད (skur smad, 'lower Kuri Chhu'), an elevational subdivision of the Kuri Chhu valley.

b_pemagatsel.first_mention_attestation: Named Pemagatsel in 1970 CE by Dudjom Rinpoche; previously known as Khoi Dung.
b_pemagatsel.etymology_analysis: From Dzongkha པདྨ་དགའ་ཚལ (pad ma dga' tshal, 'Blissful Land/Garden of the Lotus'), coined in 1970 CE by Dudjom Rinpoche to replace the older name Khoi Dung.

b_mongar.first_mention_attestation: Mongar Dzong was constructed in 1930 CE under the Second King Jigme Wangchuck to replace the older Zhongar Dzong; no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_mongar.etymology_analysis: From Dzongkha མོང་སྒར (mong sgar), the eastern Bhutanese town and district center established around Mongar Dzong in 1930 CE.

b_trongsa.first_mention_attestation: First attested with the establishment of a temple in 1543 CE by the Drukpa lama Ngagi Wangchuk, later expanded into Trongsa Dzong in 1647 CE.
b_trongsa.etymology_analysis: From Dzongkha ཀྲོང་གསར (krong gsar, 'new village'), the central Bhutanese seat of the Trongsa Penlops.

b_zhemgang.first_mention_attestation: Originated with a hermitage founded in 1163 CE by Lama Zhang Dorje Drakpa, called Zhangang ('Lama Zhang's ridge'), which evolved into Zhemgang; formal dzong built in 1655 CE.

eponym.details: Named after Lama Zhang Dorje Drakpa (1123–1193 CE), a Drukpa Kagyu master who founded a hermitage on the ridge in 1163 CE; the original name Zhangang ('Lama Zhang's ridge') evolved into Zhemgang.

b_zhemgang.etymology_analysis: From Dzongkha གཞལམ་སྒང (gzhalm sgang), evolved from Zhang-sgang ('Lama Zhang's ridge') after Lama Zhang Dorje Drakpa founded a hermitage there in 1163 CE.

b_golag.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; modern Golag Township in Zayü County, Nyingchi.
b_golag.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan མགོ་ལག (mgo lag, Chinese 古拉 Gǔlā), a township in Zayü County.

b_cawarong.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Chawalong (Cawarong) Township in Zayü County, Nyingchi.
b_cawarong.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ཚ་བ་རོང (tsha ba rong, 'hot valley/gorge'), referring to the low-elevation dry-warm Nu (Salween) River gorge in eastern Zayü County.

b_goyu.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; directional/locator compound ('head/upper land') for Goyü Township in Zayü County.
b_goyu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan མགོ་ཡུལ (mgo yul, 'head/upper land'), a directional/locator compound for Goyü Township in Zayü County.

b_rima.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Rima is attested as a border trading town in Zayul in late medieval/modern sources.
b_rima.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan རི་མ (ri ma), the historical capital and trading town of Zayul at the confluence of the Rongto Chu and Zayul Chu.

b_dzayul.first_mention_attestation: No documented contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE for the specific name rDza-yul; Phagmodrupa established Kemai Zong in 1371 CE.
b_dzayul.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan རྫ་ཡུལ (rdza yul, 'rocky/scree country'), the historical southeastern Tibetan region corresponding to Zayü County.

b_zayu.first_mention_attestation: No documented contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE; duplicate/variant barony of Zayul (rDza-yul) in c_rima.
b_zayu.etymology_analysis: Variant romanization of Tibetan རྫ་ཡུལ (rdza yul, 'rocky/scree country'), representing a separate in-game holding in Zayul.

b_roing.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for the town name Roing; nearby Bhismaknagar Fort dates to the 8th–16th century CE Chutia period, while Roing itself is a modern administrative center.
b_roing.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Idu Mishmi toponym for the headquarters of Lower Dibang Valley district in Arunachal Pradesh, India.

b_anini.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in 20th-century Indian administrative records as the headquarters of Dibang Valley district.

morphemes.translation: indigenous local settlement toponym (exact meaning unverified)

b_anini.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Idu Mishmi toponym in the upper Dibang Valley of Arunachal Pradesh.

b_tezu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in 20th-century Indian administrative records when the Mishmi Hills district headquarters moved from Sadiya to Tezu in 1952 CE.

morphemes.translation: indigenous local toponym in the Lohit valley

b_tezu.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Mishmi toponym for a settlement on the banks of the Lohit River in Arunachal Pradesh.

b_kibithu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in 20th-century Indian border and administrative surveys.
b_kibithu.etymology_analysis: Indigenous local toponym for the easternmost inhabited village on the Lohit River near the India–China–Myanmar tri-junction.

b_hawai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in modern Indian administrative records (made headquarters of Anjaw district in 2004 CE).
b_hawai.etymology_analysis: From Kaman Mishmi 'hawai', meaning 'pond', referring to a local topographic feature on the Lohit River.

b_along.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in 20th-century Indian administrative records (now officially renamed Aalo).

morphemes.translation: indigenous settlement name at the Sipu–Siyom confluence

b_along.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Adi/Galo toponym (anglicized as Along, officially Aalo) for the valley settlement in West Siang.

b_mechuka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; known prior to the 1950s CE as Pachakshiri and documented in modern Tibetan/Indian records as Menchukha.
b_mechuka.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan/Memba 'sman-chu-kha' ('medicinal water of snow'), referring to the valley's natural springs and climate.

b_tuting.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in 20th-century Indian administrative and border records.
b_tuting.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Upper Siang toponym along the Siang (Yarlung Tsangpo) trade corridor.

b_itanagar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; named after Ita Fort (dated archaeologically to the 14th–15th century CE), with the modern capital established in 1974 CE.
b_itanagar.etymology_analysis: Indo-Aryan compound meaning 'City of Bricks', named after the medieval brick-built Ita Fort (14th–15th century CE).

b_ziro.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in 20th-century Indian administrative records (made Subansiri Frontier Division headquarters in the 1950s CE).
b_ziro.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Apatani toponym for the highland plateau valley in Lower Subansiri.

b_daporijo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in 20th-century Indian administrative records (circle headquarters established in 1953 CE).

morphemes.translation: indigenous settlement toponym on the Subansiri River

b_daporijo.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Tagin toponym for a settlement on the upper Subansiri River in Arunachal Pradesh.

b_mainling.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in later Tibetan and Qing-era administrative records as sMan-gling (Mainling).
b_mainling.etymology_analysis: Tibetan 'sMan-gling' ('Land of Medicine'), referring to the rich medicinal flora of the Yarlung Tsangpo valley in Nyingchi.

b_wolong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in modern Chinese/Tibetan administrative records as a town in Mainling.
b_wolong.etymology_analysis: Sinicized administrative toponym (Wòlóng, 'Crouching Dragon') for a town in Mainling, Nyingchi.

b_medog.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; the region is attested as the 'hidden land' of Pemako (Pad-ma-bkod) in post-867 Nyingma terma literature and as Mêdog in Qing/modern Tibetan administration.
b_medog.etymology_analysis: Tibetan 'Me-tog' ('flower'), reflecting the subtropical flora of the Yarlung Tsangpo gorge; historically known as Pemako ('Lotus Array').

b_bokthang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found for this constituent toponym.
b_bokthang.etymology_analysis: Tibetic/Tshangla toponym containing the common suffix '-thang' ('plain' or 'meadow').

b_yingkiong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in 20th-century Indian administrative records as the headquarters of Upper Siang district.
b_yingkiong.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Adi toponym for the administrative town situated near the Siang River in Upper Siang.

b_chungthang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in later Sikkimese religious traditions and modern administrative records.
b_chungthang.etymology_analysis: Sikkimese/Lepcha-Tibetan toponym meaning 'the best meadows' (or 'marriage meadow'), located at the confluence of the Lachen and Lachung rivers.

b_kalimpong.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in official British Indian records in 1864–1865 CE (Ashley Eden's mission and the 1865 Treaty of Sinchula).

morphemes.translation: stockade, gathering place (or 'kaulim' fibrous plant in Lepcha)

b_kalimpong.etymology_analysis: Etymology debated: either Tibetan 'kalon-pong' ('stockade/assembly of the king's ministers') or Lepcha 'ka-lim-pong' ('ridge where we play' / 'kaulim' plant).

b_dromo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in post-867 Tibetan geographical works as Gro-mo (Dromo) and in 19th-century British accounts as Chumbi Valley.

morphemes.translation: wheat valley / warm valley (Tibetan name for the Chumbi Valley)

b_dromo.etymology_analysis: Tibetan 'Gro-mo' (pronounced Dromo or Tromo), the indigenous choronym for the Chumbi Valley between Sikkim and Bhutan.

b_daramdin.first_mention_attestation: Earliest chronological reference in Sikkimese/Limbuwan traditional chronicles places Chief Na Hang of Daramdin around 870 CE (post-867 CE), with no contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_daramdin.etymology_analysis: Indigenous West Sikkim toponym associated with early Limbu and Lepcha chieftaincies.

b_darjeeling.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1829 CE in British East India Company survey reports by Captain G.A. Lloyd and J.W. Grant (leased from Sikkim in 1835 CE).
b_darjeeling.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Tibetan 'rDo-rje-gling' ('Land of the Thunderbolt'), originally referring to a Buddhist monastery on Observatory Hill.

b_paro.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; while Kyichu Lhakhang in the valley is traditionally dated to 659 CE, the toponym sPa-gro/sPa-ro is first attested in post-867 medieval Tibetan chronicles and terma texts.

morphemes.translation: historic western Bhutanese valley name (traditional etymologies: 'ornamental/fertile' or 'bamboo-wheat')

b_paro.etymology_analysis: Dzongkha 'sPa-ro' (Classical Tibetan 'sPa-gro'), the historic choronym of the fertile Paro Valley in western Bhutan.

b_thimpu.first_mention_attestation: Earliest dated architectural/historical record in the Thimphu valley is the founding of Dho-Ngon Dzong in 1216 CE by Lama Gyalwa Lhanangpa (later rebuilt as Tashichho Dzong in 1641 CE).

morphemes.translation: sunken/inner valley (traditional etymology from Thimphu valley)

b_thimpu.etymology_analysis: Dzongkha 'Thim-phug', referring to the western central valley along the Wang Chhu; became Bhutan's capital in 1955–1961 CE.

b_daga.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1648–1651 CE when Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal ordered Dronyer Druk Namgyel to construct Daga Trashiyangtse Dzong.

morphemes.translation: realm/place of white prayer flags (from Darkala/Darkarnang)

b_daga.etymology_analysis: Dzongkha 'Dar-dkar-na' (Daga/Dagana), derived from 'Darkala' and 'Darkarnang' ('Realm of White Prayer Flags').

b_sarpang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Bhutanese administrative records.
b_sarpang.etymology_analysis: Dzongkha 'gSar-spang' ('New Meadow'), referring to the southern foothill plain in Bhutan.

b_punakha.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1637–1638 CE with the construction of Punakha Dzong (Pungtang Dechen Phodrang) by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal.

morphemes.translation: palace/valley of heaped-up happiness (shortened from Pungtang Dechen Phodrang)

b_punakha.etymology_analysis: Dzongkha 'sPu-na-kha', associated with Pungtang Dechen Phodrang ('Palace of Great Happiness') at the confluence of the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu.

b_gasa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested <= 867 CE; mentioned in 13th-century Drukpa Kagyu hagiographies and documented in 1656–1657 CE during the Bhutan–Tibet war and the building of Gasa Dzong.

morphemes.translation: land/camp of the blacksmith (or joyful place, dga'-sa)

b_gasa.etymology_analysis: Dzongkha 'mGar-sa', the northernmost highland district of Bhutan guarding the route to Tibet.

b_sumdo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in 19th–20th century British/Chinese geographical surveys of Aksai Chin near the upper Karakash headwaters.
b_sumdo.etymology_analysis: Tibetan/Ladakhi 'gSum-mdo' ('Three-Way Confluence'), a descriptive topographic name in Aksai Chin.

b_chungtash.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in 19th–20th century Yarkand–Leh caravan route records.
b_chungtash.etymology_analysis: Yarkandi Turkic 'Chong-tash' ('Big Stone'), a caravan halting landmark on the Ladakh–Yarkand trade route.

b_thaldat.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1868 CE by British Joint Commissioner Henry Cayley (and traversed by Adolphe Schlagintweit in 1857 CE and W.H. Johnson in 1865 CE).

morphemes.translation: ice or snow ground (per Henry Cayley, 1868 CE)

b_thaldat.etymology_analysis: Ladakhi/Tibetan toponym recorded by Henry Cayley in 1868 CE as meaning 'Ice or Snow Ground', referring to the salt/snow basin in Aksai Chin (modern Tianshuihai).

b_sumnal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in 19th-century European geographical surveys of the Karakash River (e.g., Élisée Reclus, 1882 CE).

morphemes.translation: high-altitude halting place on the upper Karakash River

b_sumnal.etymology_analysis: Caravan halting point on the upper Karakash River in Aksai Chin.

b_khaplu.first_mention_attestation: Earliest written mention of Khaplu appears in Mirza Haidar Dughlat's Tarikh-i-Rashidi (c. 1546 CE), though the Yabgo dynasty kingdom likely emerged around the 10th century CE.
b_khaplu.etymology_analysis: Balti toponym for the historic capital of the Yabgo dynasty along the Shyok River in eastern Baltistan.

b_haldi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented only in modern Pakistani/Baltistan geographical and hydrological records.

morphemes.translation: village toponym in the lower Hushe Valley, Ghanche

b_haldi.etymology_analysis: Balti village toponym located on an alluvial fan in the lower Hushe Valley near Khaplu.

b_shigar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; local Amacha dynasty traditions begin in the 10th century CE, with extant Islamic monuments (Amburiq Mosque) from the 14th century CE and Shigar Fort from the 17th century CE.

morphemes.translation: historic Balti valley and fortress town

b_shigar.etymology_analysis: Balti toponym for the valley and historic seat of the Amacha dynasty in Baltistan.

b_askole.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first documented in 19th–20th century Karakoram mountaineering and survey accounts.

morphemes.translation: high-altitude village toponym in the Braldo Valley

b_askole.etymology_analysis: Balti toponym for the highest permanent settlement in the Braldo Valley before the Baltoro Glacier.

b_skardu.first_mention_attestation: Earliest written mention is 'Askardu' in Mirza Haidar Dughlat's Tarikh-i-Rashidi (first half of the 16th century CE, c. 1546 CE); Maqpon Bokha founded Skardu as his capital around 1500 CE.

morphemes.translation: lowland between two high places (or star-gate/valley-mouth)

b_skardu.etymology_analysis: Balti 'sKar-mdo', traditionally interpreted as 'a lowland between two high places' (referring to Shigar and Satpara Lake).

historical_names.name: Great Bolor
historical_names.source: Xuanzang's Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (c. 646 CE) and Tang dynastic histories (Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang, 7th–8th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Baltistan / the Skardu basin is prominently attested in 7th–8th century CE Tang sources (and Gao Xianzhi's 747 CE campaign) as Great Bolor / Palola prior to Maqpon Bokha's foundation of Skardu c. 1500 CE.

historical_names.name: Palola
historical_names.source: Xuanzang's Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (c. 646 CE) and Tang dynastic histories (Old Book of Tang / New Book of Tang, 7th–8th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Baltistan / the Skardu basin is prominently attested in 7th–8th century CE Tang sources (and Gao Xianzhi's 747 CE campaign) as Great Bolor / Palola prior to Maqpon Bokha's foundation of Skardu c. 1500 CE.

b_roundu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in post-medieval Balti dynastic traditions (branch of the Maqpon dynasty after c. 1600 CE) and modern records.
b_roundu.etymology_analysis: Balti toponym for the gorge valley on the Indus River between Skardu and Gilgit.

b_tolti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in early modern Balti/Ladakhi history and the 1840 CE Dogra conquest.
b_tolti.etymology_analysis: Balti toponym for a historic settlement and fort along the Indus River in Kharmang.

b_gultari.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Gilgit-Baltistan administrative records.

morphemes.translation: highland valley toponym south of Skardu

b_gultari.etymology_analysis: Balti/Shina toponym for the remote highland valley near the Deosai plateau.

b_dhankar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Dhankar Gompa and the seat of the Nonos of Spiti are dated to the 11th–17th centuries CE.
b_dhankar.etymology_analysis: From Spiti Bhoti/Tibetan 'Dhang-khar' ('Fort on a Cliff'), describing the fortified monastery overlooking the Spiti–Pin river confluence.

b_tabo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 996 CE (Tibetan Fire Ape year) in the foundation inscriptions of Tabo Monastery established by Yeshe-Ö and Rinchen Zangpo.
b_tabo.etymology_analysis: Tibetan/Spiti Bhoti toponym for the monastic village in Spiti Valley, attested from the 996 CE foundation of Tabo Chos-khor.

b_kardang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Kardang Monastery in Lahaul is traditionally dated to the 12th century CE.

morphemes.translation: historic Lahaul valley village and monastery toponym

b_kardang.etymology_analysis: Tibetic/Lahauli toponym for the former capital village and Drukpa monastery on the Bhaga River.

b_kamru.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; mentioned in later genealogies and traditions of the Bushahr state (from the 15th century CE onward).

morphemes.translation: settlement name associated in local tradition with Kamakhya (Kamarupa)

b_kamru.etymology_analysis: Kamru is a historic village and fort in the Sangla (Baspa) Valley of Kinnaur, formerly the capital of the Bushahr principality. Local priestly tradition holds that its earlier name was Mone and that it was renamed Kamru after the installation of the goddess Kamakhya Devi (associated with Kamarupa).

b_kalpa.first_mention_attestation: Known as Chini until the mid-20th century; renamed Kalpa around 1960–1962 CE during the reorganization of Kinnaur District.
b_kalpa.etymology_analysis: Kalpa is a village in the Sutlej Valley of Kinnaur that was historically known as Chini until after Indian independence (c. 1960–1962 CE). Neither the modern name Kalpa nor the earlier name Chini has a documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_poo.first_mention_attestation: Early 11th-century CE Tibetan inscriptions at Pooh (Tibetan: sPu) associated with the Guge kingdom and the translator Rinchen Zangpo (958–1055 CE).

morphemes.translation: upper / head of a valley (toponymic root of Poo/Pooh)

b_poo.etymology_analysis: Poo (Pooh, also Spuwa; Tibetan sPu) is a town in Upper Kinnaur near the Tibetan border. Early 11th-century CE Tibetan inscriptions attest sPu as an important trading and religious center in the Western Himalayan realm of Guge, postdating the 867 CE baseline.

b_nako.first_mention_attestation: 11th-century CE monastic foundation (Nako Monastery / Lotsava Lhakhang, traditionally dated c. 1025 CE and attributed to Rinchen Zangpo).

morphemes.translation: high-altitude village and lake settlement in Upper Kinnaur

b_nako.etymology_analysis: Nako is a high-altitude village beside Nako Lake in Upper Kinnaur. Its Buddhist temple complex is dated to the 11th–12th century CE (traditionally c. 1025 CE under Rinchen Zangpo), with no extant written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_demchok.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as Demchok Karpo in the 17th-century Ladakh Chronicles (La-dvags-rgyal-rabs) in its account of the c. 930 CE partition of Kyide Nyimagon's kingdom to Palgyigon, and in the 1684 CE Treaty of Tingmosgang.
b_demchok.etymology_analysis: Demchok (Tibetan: bDe-mchog, 'Supreme Bliss', the Tibetan name of the Tantric deity Cakrasaṃvara) is named after Demchok Karpo (Demchok Lhari Karpo), the white sacred peak behind the settlement. Its earliest historical reference is to the 10th-century CE partition of Maryul (c. 930 CE) in the Ladakh Chronicles.

b_hanle.first_mention_attestation: 17th-century CE Ladakhi history: King Sengge Namgyal died at Hanle in 1642 CE, and Hanle Monastery was founded in the 17th century CE.

morphemes.translation: valley and monastic settlement in southeastern Ladakh

b_hanle.etymology_analysis: Hanle is a high-altitude settlement in the Changthang region of Ladakh, best known for the 17th-century CE Drukpa Kagyu Hanle Monastery and as the place where King Sengge Namgyal died in 1642 CE. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_chusul.first_mention_attestation: Documented in 1842 CE in connection with the Battle of Chushul and the Treaty of Chushul during the Dogra–Tibetan War.
b_chusul.etymology_analysis: Chushul (Chusul; Tibetan chu-shul, 'wet land' or 'marshy water-course') is a border village in eastern Ladakh. Local tradition recalls an earlier name Taklung Diskit, and the earliest datable written records are from the 1842 CE Dogra–Tibetan War.

b_diskit.first_mention_attestation: 15th-century CE foundation of Diskit Monastery (c. 1420 CE) by Changzem Tserab Zangpo, disciple of Je Tsongkhapa.
b_diskit.etymology_analysis: Diskit (Tibetan: bDe-skyid, 'peace and happiness') is the main town of the Nubra Valley in Ladakh. While post-Kushan ceramics (4th–8th century CE) have been found at nearby Tingang ruins, the toponym Diskit is attested from the 15th-century CE foundation of Diskit Monastery.

b_panamik.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; recorded in modern Ladakhi administrative and travel records.
b_panamik.etymology_analysis: Panamik (Panamic) is a town in the Nubra Valley of Ladakh known for its hot springs. Its name is a contraction of Tibetan spang-na chu-mig ('the spring in the meadows'), and it has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_turtuk.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested in later Balti and Ladakhi historical traditions and modern records.

morphemes.translation: settlement name (glossed locally as 'desire to stay')

b_turtuk.etymology_analysis: Turtuk is a Balti-speaking village in the Shyok Valley (historically part of Baltistan, under Indian administration since 1971 CE). There is no documented written attestation of the name <= 867 CE.

b_dipsang.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; depicted as Depsang Plains on early 20th-century Survey of India maps (e.g., 1916 CE).
b_dipsang.etymology_analysis: Dipsang (Depsang) refers to the high-altitude Depsang Plains in northern Ladakh. According to Tibetan etymology, Depsang means 'open, elevated plain'; the feature has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_khurnak.first_mention_attestation: Described as ruins by Henry Haversham Godwin-Austen in the 1860s CE; Khurnak Fort is dated in modern accounts to c. 1867 CE.
b_khurnak.etymology_analysis: Khurnak (Tibetan: mKhar-nag, 'Black Fort') is a ruined fort on the northern shore of Pangong Tso. It is first documented in 19th-century CE British survey reports (Godwin-Austen) with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_nischu.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in 1857 CE when Adolf Schlagintweit traversed the Chang Chenmo route via Gogra to Nischu and Aksai Chin.
b_nischu.etymology_analysis: Nischu is a high-altitude halting spot on the Chang Chenmo route between Ladakh and Aksai Chin, first documented in 19th-century CE exploration records (Adolf Schlagintweit, 1857 CE).

b_sumna.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; appears only in modern geographical and pastoralist records of the Karakoram–Aksai Chin corridor.
b_sumna.etymology_analysis: Sumna is a remote high-altitude location in the Ladakh–Aksai Chin borderlands along the Karakoram trade corridor. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_leh.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 17th-century Ladakh Chronicles (La-dvags-rgyal-rabs) in connection with the 10th-century CE establishment of Maryul (c. 930 CE) and later Namgyal-era constructions; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_leh.etymology_analysis: Leh (Ladakhi: sLe, originally sLes) derives from Tibetan sles ('nomad encampment' or 'pastureland'). While the Leh valley has older Dardic ruins ('Brog-pal-mkhar), the toponym itself has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_shey.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 17th-century Ladakh Chronicles (La-dvags-rgyal-rabs) as the seat/capital of Kyide Nyimagon and Lhachen Palgyigon's kingdom of Maryul (c. 930 CE).
b_shey.etymology_analysis: Shey (Tibetan: Shel, 'crystal' or 'mirror') was the first capital of the West Tibetan kingdom of Maryul established around 930 CE, postdating the 867 CE baseline.

b_khalatse.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Ladakh Chronicles (La-dvags-rgyal-rabs) for the reign of King Lhachen Naglug (c. 1150–1175 CE), who built Bragnag castle and the bridge at Khalatse; the c. 100–110 CE Kushan Kharoṣṭhī inscription at the site names Vima Kadphises but not the toponym Khalatse.
b_khalatse.etymology_analysis: Khalatse (Wylie: mkhar la rtse, 'fortress on the pass/peak', also Kha-la-rtse) is a strategic Indus crossing in Lower Ladakh. Although a 1st–2nd century CE Kushan inscription of Vima Kadphises stands near the bridge, it does not record the name Khalatse, which is first attested in the 12th century CE under Lhachen Naglug.

b_tangtse.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE for the toponym Tangtse (Brang-rtse); 9th–10th century CE Sogdian and Arabic traveler inscriptions on boulders near the village do not record the settlement name.
b_tangtse.etymology_analysis: Tangtse or Drangtse (Tibetan: Brang-rtse) is a village in Changthang, Ladakh. Although boulders near Tangtse preserve 9th–10th century CE Sogdian and Arabic inscriptions and Nestorian crosses, those traveler graffiti do not attest the Tibetan toponym Brang-rtse <= 867 CE.

b_memar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested in modern Tibetan gazetteers and geographical surveys of Rutog County.
b_memar.etymology_analysis: Memar (Tibetan: Me-dmar, 'Red Fire') corresponds to the Memar Co (Me-dmar mtsho) lake basin in Rutog County, Ngari, Tibet. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_bangdag.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Bangda Lake (Bangdag Co) in Rutog County is documented in 20th-century CE surveys and Chinese-Tibetan geographical records.

morphemes.translation: toponym associated with Bangda Lake (Bangdag Co)

b_bangdag.etymology_analysis: Bangdag refers to the Bangdag Co (Bangda Lake) area in Rutog County, Ngari, Tibet. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_bairab.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Bairab Co (Tibetan: dPal-rab mtsho) is attested in modern Chinese-Tibetan gazetteers (1981–1995 CE).
b_bairab.etymology_analysis: Bairab (Tibetan: dPal-rab, 'Supreme Splendor') corresponds to Bairab Co (dPal-rab mtsho) in Rutog County, Ngari, Tibet. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_rutog.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Ladakh Chronicles (La-dvags-rgyal-rabs) as part of Lhachen Palgyigon's 10th-century CE inheritance (c. 930 CE), and in later Bonpo histories of Zhangzhung; no contemporary written document <= 867 CE attests the name Ru-thog.
b_rutog.etymology_analysis: Rutog or Rudok (Tibetan: Ru-thog) is the historic capital of the Rudok region in Ngari, Western Tibet. Although prehistoric rock art in Rutog County dates back millennia and later Bonpo texts mention Ru-thog seng-ge rdzong in Zhangzhung, the earliest datable historical reference to the toponym is the 10th-century CE division of Maryul (c. 930 CE).

b_risum.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested as Risum Township (Tibetan: Ri-gsum shang) in modern Rutog County records.
b_risum.etymology_analysis: Risum (Tibetan: Ri-gsum, 'Three Mountains') is a township in Rutog County, Ngari, Tibet. While ancient rock paintings exist at Risum Rimodong, the toponym Risum has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_rebang.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested as Rebang Township (Rabang) in modern Rutog County administrative records.

morphemes.translation: settlement and lake-basin name in Rutog

b_rebang.etymology_analysis: Rebang (Rabang) is a township and lake-basin locality (Rebang Co) in Rutog County, Ngari, Tibet. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_changmar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; recorded in modern geographical gazetteers of Rutog County.
b_changmar.etymology_analysis: Changmar (Tibetan: Byang-dmar, 'Red North') is a settlement in northern Rutog County, Ngari, Tibet. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_darcha.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; known in regional Lahaul history and trade-fair traditions (La Darcha).

morphemes.translation: village and trade-halting place in northern Lahaul

b_darcha.etymology_analysis: Darcha is the northernmost village in Lahaul along the Bhaga River and the historic trade route toward Zanskar and Ladakh. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_karzok.first_mention_attestation: Korzok Monastery and settlement are attested from the 18th–19th century CE (roughly 300 years old in local tradition, c. 1840s CE).
b_karzok.etymology_analysis: Karzok (Korzok) is a high-altitude Changpa settlement on the northwestern shore of Tso Moriri in Ladakh. Local Changpa tradition derives the name from kor (livestock owned by the gompa) and zok (where goods are stored); it has no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_padum.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Padum is attested in medieval Zanskari and Ladakhi chronicles (10th century CE onward) and traditionally named after the 8th-century CE master Padmasambhava.

morphemes.translation: town name traditionally derived from Padmasambhava

b_padum.etymology_analysis: Padum is the main town and historic capital of Zanskar. Local tradition attributes its name to the 8th-century CE Buddhist master Padmasambhava (pre-867 CE), though the settlement itself has no contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_zangla.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested in medieval Zanskari royal history and later Ladakhi chronicles.
b_zangla.etymology_analysis: Zangla (Tibetan: Zangs-la, reflecting zangs 'copper') is a historic village and former royal seat in Zanskar, Ladakh. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_lingshet.first_mention_attestation: Lingshed Monastery was founded in the 1440s CE by Changsems Sherabs Zangpo, and the village (Ling-snyed) is recorded in the Ladakh Chronicles for c. 1500 CE.
b_lingshet.etymology_analysis: Lingshet (Lingshed; Tibetan: Gling-snyed) is a remote monastic village in Ladakh between Zanskar and Khalatse. Its Gelugpa monastery was founded in the 1440s CE, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_purig.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Purig (Pu-rig) is attested in later Ladakhi and Balti chronicles and early modern histories.

morphemes.translation: regional name (variously glossed as 'of Tibetan origin' or 'tubular valley')

b_purig.etymology_analysis: Purig (Purik) is the historical region corresponding to much of modern Kargil district in western Ladakh. Although Central Asian-influenced ceramics in Purig date to the 1st–7th centuries CE, the toponym Purig has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_dras.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested in early modern and modern Kashmiri and Ladakhi records.
b_dras.etymology_analysis: Dras (Drass, locally Hembabs) is a town in Kargil district, Ladakh, on the trade route below Zoji La. While Kushan-era pottery has been found in the area, the name Dras has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_caze.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested as Cazê / Zazê Township (Tibetan: Tshwa-rtse) in modern Ngamring County records.
b_caze.etymology_analysis: Caze (Cazê / Zazê; Tibetan: Tshwa-rtse) is a high-altitude township in Ngamring County, Shigatse, Tibet. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_rusar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested as Rusar Township (Tibetan: Ru-gsar shang) in modern Ngamring County records.
b_rusar.etymology_analysis: Rusar (Tibetan: Ru-gsar, 'New Wing/Division') is a township in Ngamring County, Shigatse, Tibet. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_kunglung.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested as Kunglung Township (Tibetan: Gung-lung shang) in modern Ngamring County records.
b_kunglung.etymology_analysis: Kunglung (Gunglung; Tibetan: Gung-lung, 'Middle Valley') is a township in Ngamring County, Shigatse, Tibet. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_kagar.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested as Kagar Town (Tibetan: Gad-sgang), the modern county seat of Ngamring County.
b_kagar.etymology_analysis: Kagar (Tibetan: Gad-sgang) is the administrative seat of Ngamring County in Shigatse, Tibet. While Ngamring Monastery nearby was founded in 1225 CE, Kagar itself has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_sangsang.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested as Sangsang Town (Tibetan: bZang-bzang) in Ngamring County.
b_sangsang.etymology_analysis: Sangsang (Tibetan: bZang-bzang) is a town in Ngamring County, Shigatse, Tibet. Nearby Zangzang Lhadrak cave is associated in later Treasure (gter-ma) tradition with Padmasambhava, but the town Sangsang has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_quog.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested as Qu'og Township (Tibetan: Chu-'og shang) in modern Ngamring County records.
b_quog.etymology_analysis: Quog (Qu'og; Tibetan: Chu-'og, 'Below the Water') is a township in Ngamring County, Shigatse, Tibet. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_goingyibug.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested as Gönkyibuk / Goin'gyibug (Tibetan: dGon-skyid-sbug) in modern Ngamring County records.
b_goingyibug.etymology_analysis: Goingyibug (Goin'gyibug / Gönkyibuk; Tibetan: dGon-skyid-sbug, 'Happy Monastery Hollow') is a township in Ngamring County, Shigatse, Tibet. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_tongmoin.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; Xaitongmoin (bZhad-mthong-smon) is attested from the 11th century CE onward (monasteries founded 1050 CE) and Tongmoin Township in modern Shigatse records.
b_tongmoin.etymology_analysis: Tongmoin (Tibetan: mThong-smon, 'Joy/Aspiration at Sight') is a township in Xaitongmoin County, Shigatse, Tibet. Its earliest monastic institutions in the county date to 1050 CE, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_qingtu.first_mention_attestation: No documented written attestation <= 867 CE; attested as Qingtü Township (Tibetan: Byin-mthu shang) in modern Xaitongmoin County records.
b_qingtu.etymology_analysis: Qingtu (Qingtü; Tibetan: Byin-mthu, 'Power of Blessing') is a township in Xaitongmoin County, Shigatse, Tibet. It has no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_leba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Lêba Township in Xaitongmoin County, Shigatse.
b_leba.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan sle pa (སླེ་པ), a local settlement name in Xaitongmoin County; no pre-867 CE historical attestation is known.

b_kungtang.first_mention_attestation: Attested in post-867 CE Tibetan historiography as the seat of Mangyul Gungthang (10th–11th century CE, including Depal Khortsen's line c. 910 CE and Milarepa's birthplace in the 11th century CE); unattested <= 867 CE.
b_kungtang.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan gung thang (གུང་ཐང), meaning 'middle plain', referring to the high valley plain in upper Gyirong/Dzongka.

b_gyirong.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation of the specific Tibetan toponym 'Skyid-grong' (Gyirong) <= 867 CE; Kyirong Chöde dates to the 10th century CE and Atisha visited in the 11th century CE (the nearby 658 CE Tang inscription of Wang Xuance does not record this Tibetan name).
b_gyirong.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan skyid grong (སྐྱིད་གྲོང), meaning 'happy village' or 'pleasant settlement', reflecting the mild climate of the lower Gyirong valley.

historical_names.name: Xiao Yangtong
historical_names.source: Da Tang Tianzhu shi chu ming (658 CE Tang rock inscription north of Dzongka)
historical_names.notes: Wang Xuance's 658 CE Tang Dynasty rock inscription in the Gyirong corridor records Xiao Yangtong, and Mangyul is attested in Old Tibetan records.

historical_names.name: Mangyul
historical_names.source: Da Tang Tianzhu shi chu ming (658 CE Tang rock inscription north of Dzongka)
historical_names.notes: Wang Xuance's 658 CE Tang Dynasty rock inscription in the Gyirong corridor records Xiao Yangtong, and Mangyul is attested in Old Tibetan records.

b_chagne.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Drakna (Chagnê) Township in Gyirong County, Shigatse.
b_chagne.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan brag sne / brag sna (བྲག་སྣེ / བྲག་སྣ), meaning 'cliff spur' or 'rocky promontory', rendered in PRC Tibetan Pinyin as Chagnê.

b_kyakyaru.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan geographical and administrative records as the alternative name of Saga Town in Saga County, Shigatse.
b_kyakyaru.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan skya skya ru, a local district/settlement name associated with Saga Town in Shigatse.

b_changgo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Changgo Township in Saga County, Shigatse.
b_changgo.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan 'phrang sgo (འཕྲང་སྒོ), meaning 'narrow pass gate' or 'entrance to a mountain defile'.

b_lhagcang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Lhagcang Township in Saga County, Shigatse.
b_lhagcang.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan lhag tshang (ལྷག་ཚང), a local settlement and township name in Saga County.

b_tsongdu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; 'Tsongdu' (tshong 'dus) is recorded in later Tibetan and trans-Himalayan trade history as the historical name of Nyalam Town.
b_tsongdu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan tshong 'dus (ཚོང་འདུས), meaning 'market' or 'trading assembly', reflecting Nyalam's role as a trans-Himalayan trade hub.

b_mainpu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Mainpu Township in Nyalam County, Shigatse.
b_mainpu.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan sman phu (སྨན་ཕུ), meaning 'upper valley of medicinal herbs'.

b_tingri.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Tibetan Buddhist historiography in connection with the Indian master Padampa Sangye's residence and teaching at Tingri Langkhor (c. 1097–1117 CE, Blue Annals).
b_tingri.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan ding ri (དིང་རི), an oronymic compound with ri ('mountain/hill'), traditionally associated with the hill/plain north of Everest.

b_shelkar.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1266 CE with the founding of Shelkar Chode Monastery (and later Shelkar Dorje Dzong); unattested <= 867 CE.
b_shelkar.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan shel dkar (ཤེལ་དཀར), meaning 'white crystal', referring to the pale crystal-like rock hill above the town.

b_sagya.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1073 CE when Khön Könchok Gyalpo founded Sakya Monastery on the pale-earth hillside; unattested <= 867 CE.
b_sagya.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan sa skya (ས་སྐྱ), meaning 'pale earth', referring to the light-colored soil of the Ponpori hillside where Sakya Monastery was built.

b_se.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Së (Srad) Township in Sa'gya County, Shigatse.
b_se.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan srad / se (སྲད / སེ), a local valley and township name in Sa'gya County.

b_lhaze.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in post-867 CE Tibetan monastic and dzong records (Lhatse County, Shigatse).
b_lhaze.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan lha rtse (ལྷ་རྩེ), meaning 'divine peak', an oronymic name for the rocky summit and dzong site.

b_kamba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in later Tibetan administrative and geographical records (Kamba County, Shigatse).
b_kamba.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan gam pa (གམ་པ), a local settlement and county name in southern Shigatse bordering Sikkim.

b_dinggye.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in later Tibetan administrative and geographical records (Dinggyê County, Shigatse).
b_dinggye.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan gding skyes / gting skyes (གདིང་སྐྱེས / གཏིང་སྐྱེས), a local settlement and county name in southern Shigatse.

b_gyangze.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1365 CE with the foundation of Gyantse Dzong and the town by Phagpa Pal Sangpo (later Pelkhor Chode Monastery in 1418 CE); earlier 9th-century associations are retrospective/legendary.
b_gyangze.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan rgyal rtse (རྒྱལ་རྩེ), meaning 'victory peak', referring to the rocky hilltop overlooking the Nyang Chu valley.

b_rinbung.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 14th–15th century CE (Rinpung Dzong under the Phagmodrupa and seat of the Rinpungpa princes from 1435 CE); unattested <= 867 CE.
b_rinbung.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan rin spungs (རིན་སྤུངས), meaning 'heap of jewels', an auspicious name for the fortress and district.

b_kangmar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in later Tibetan administrative and geographical records (Kangmar County, Shigatse).
b_kangmar.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan khang dmar (ཁང་དམར), meaning 'red house', a settlement and county name in southeastern Shigatse.

b_kamru_2.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Kamru Township in Kangmar County, Shigatse.
b_kamru_2.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan gam ru (གམ་རུ), a local township name in Kangmar County.

b_xigaze.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 1360 CE with the construction of Samzhubzê Dzong (Shiga Samzhubzê) under the Phagmodrupa regime; unattested as Shigatse <= 867 CE.
b_xigaze.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan gzhis ka rtse (གཞིས་ཀ་རྩེ), meaning 'manor peak' or 'the finest manor', shortened from Shiga Samzhubzê.

b_nyamo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Nyamo Township in Samzhubzê District, Shigatse.
b_nyamo.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan nya mo (ཉ་མོ), a local settlement and township name in Samzhubzê District.

b_banam.first_mention_attestation: Modern form 'Pa-snam' (Banam/Bainang) is unattested <= 867 CE, though its Old Tibetan predecessor 'Tsanggi Barnanggang' is attested in 676 CE in the Old Tibetan Annals.
b_banam.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan pa snam (པ་སྣམ), modern name of Bainang County, corresponding to the Old Tibetan site Tsanggi Barnanggang.

historical_names.name: Tsanggi Barnanggang
historical_names.source: Old Tibetan Annals (676 CE, death of Emperor Mangsong Mangtsen)
historical_names.notes: Emperor Mangsong Mangtsen died at Tsanggi Barnanggang (modern Bainang County) in 676 CE according to the Old Tibetan Annals.

b_namling.first_mention_attestation: The administrative name 'Rnam-gling' (Namling) is unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in post-imperial Tibetan religious and administrative records.
b_namling.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan rnam gling (རྣམ་གླིང), meaning 'complete sanctuary/park', the modern administrative name of the Oyuk, Tobgyet, and Shang valleys.

b_tobgyai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in later Tibetan geographical and administrative records as Tobgyai Township in Namling County, Shigatse.
b_tobgyai.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan thob rgyal (ཐོབ་རྒྱལ), a valley and township name in Namling County.

b_cozhelhoma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern directional administrative division ('Southern Tsodrel') in Shuanghu County, Nagqu.
b_cozhelhoma.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan tsho 'brel lho ma (ཚོ་འབྲེལ་ལྷོ་མ), a directional compound ('Southern Connected Lake / Southern Tsodrel') in Shuanghu County.

b_xibde.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Xibdê (Zhide) Township in Shuanghu County, Nagqu.
b_xibde.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan zhi bde (ཞི་བདེ), meaning 'peace and happiness', a modern township name in Shuanghu County.

b_cozhedangma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern directional administrative division ('Northern Tsodrel') in Shuanghu County, Nagqu.
b_cozhedangma.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan mtsho sbrel byang ma (ཚོ་སྦྲེལ་བྱང་མ), a directional compound ('Northern Connected Lake / Northern Tsodrel') in Shuanghu County.

b_garco.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Garco Township in Shuanghu County, Nagqu.
b_garco.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan dkar mtsho (དཀར་མཚོ), meaning 'white lake', a hydronymic name in Shuanghu County.

b_parling.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Parling Township in Shuanghu County, Nagqu.
b_parling.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan bar gling (བར་གླིང), meaning 'middle meadow/land', a modern township name in Shuanghu County.

b_dorsoidong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan toponymy and geographical surveys as Dorsoidong Co in Shuanghu County, Nagqu.
b_dorsoidong.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan gdor zol gdong mtsho (གདོར་ཟོལ་གདོང་མཚོ), the name of a major glacier-fed lake in the central Tibetan Plateau.

b_garkung.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan geographical surveys as Garkung Caka salt lake in Nagqu.
b_garkung.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan dkar khung (དཀར་ཁུང), meaning 'white hollow/cavity', shortened from the salt lake name Garkung Caka (dkar khung tshwa kha).

b_margai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan geographical surveys as Margai Caka salt lake in Changtang, Nagqu.
b_margai.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan dmar gad (དམར་གད), meaning 'red cliff/bank', shortened from the salt lake name Margai Caka (dmar gad tshwa kha).

b_yurba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan geographical surveys as Yurba Co (Yurba Tso) in Nagqu.
b_yurba.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan g.yur rba (གཡུར་རྦ), shortened from the lake name Yurba Co (g.yur rba mtsho) in northern Nagqu.

b_sewa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan geographical and administrative gazetteers (Sêwa, Nagqu).
b_sewa.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan se ba (སེ་བ), meaning 'wild rose' or 'briar', used as a local place name in Nagqu.

b_dokecoring.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan geographical and glaciological surveys as Dogai Coring lake in Nagqu.
b_dokecoring.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan rdo skas mtsho ring (རྡོ་སྐས་མཚོ་རིང), meaning 'stone-steps long lake', a major salt lake in Nagqu.

b_yuyico.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan geographical gazetteers as Yuyi Co lake in Nagqu.
b_yuyico.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan g.yu yi mtsho (གཡུ་ཡི་མཚོ), meaning 'turquoise lake'.

b_dokecoring_qangco.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern directional hydronym ('Dogai Coring North Lake') in Nagqu.
b_dokecoring_qangco.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan rdo skas mtsho ring byang mtsho (རྡོ་སྐས་མཚོ་རིང་བྱང་མཚོ), a directional compound meaning 'Dogai Coring North Lake'.

b_damquka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern administrative seat of Damxung County ('Damquka', by the Dam River).
b_damquka.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan 'dam chu kha (འདམ་ཆུ་ཁ), meaning 'on the bank of the Dam River', the modern seat of Damxung County.

b_nyinhzhong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Tibetan administrative gazetteers as Nyingzhung Township in Damxung County, Lhasa.
b_nyinhzhong.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan snying drung (སྙིང་དྲུང), a modern township name in Damxung County.

b_yangpachen.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 1500 CE with the construction of Yangpachen Monastery by the 4th Shamarpa (murals painted in 1506 CE); unattested <= 867 CE.
b_yangpachen.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan yangs pa can (ཡངས་པ་ཅན), meaning 'the spacious one', rendering Sanskrit Vaiśālī and applied to the monastery and valley.

b_gyama.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written or epigraphic attestation <= 867 CE; later Tibetan chronicles retrospectively identify Gyama Palace (Rgya ma Mingyur Ling) as built by Namri Songtsen (c. 580 CE) and the birthplace of Songtsen Gampo.
b_gyama.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Rgya ma (རྒྱ་མ), an early imperial valley and palace site in Meldro (Mal dro), birthplace of Emperor Songtsen Gampo.

b_kunggar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern town and county seat (གུང་དཀར, Gongka) of Maizhokunggar County in Lhasa.
b_kunggar.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Gung dkar (གུང་དཀར, 'white center'), modern administrative seat of Maizhokunggar County.

b_drigung.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1179 CE by Kyobpa Jigten Sumgön as Drigung Thil Monastery (འབྲི་གུང་མཐིལ), the main seat of the Drikung Kagyu lineage.
b_drigung.etymology_analysis: Tibetan 'Bri gung (འབྲི་གུང), valley and monastic seat in Maizhokunggar founded in 1179 CE.

b_paga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; constituent Tibetan settlement in the Maizhokunggar/Gyama area.
b_paga.etymology_analysis: Tibetan settlement name Paga/Baga of uncertain orthography, attested only in post-imperial/modern local usage.

b_mila_tibet.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; corresponds to Mila Mountain / Mila Pass (མི་ལ་རི) between Maizhokunggar and Gongbo'gyamda.
b_mila_tibet.etymology_analysis: Tibetan oronym Mi la (མི་ལ), naming the high mountain and pass on the eastern border of Maizhokunggar.

b_potala.first_mention_attestation: The modern Potala Palace (named after Mount Potalaka) was begun in 1645 CE by the Fifth Dalai Lama on the site of Songtsen Gampo's 7th-century Red Hill fortress.

morphemes.translation: Mount Potalaka, mythical abode of Avalokiteśvara

b_potala.etymology_analysis: Named after Sanskrit Mount Potalaka, sacred abode of Avalokiteśvara; applied to the palace complex begun in 1645 CE on Marpo Ri.

historical_names.name: Marpo Ri
historical_names.source: Tibetan imperial tradition attributing Songtsen Gampo's 637 CE fortress/palace to Marpo Ri ('Red Hill')
historical_names.notes: Songtsen Gampo built an earlier palace on Marpo Ri ('Red Hill') c. 637 CE before the 1645 CE Potala Palace.

b_lhasa.first_mention_attestation: First recorded by the name Lhasa (ལྷ་ས, referring to the Jowo temple) in the Sino-Tibetan treaty inscription of 822 CE.
b_lhasa.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Lha sa (ལྷ་ས, 'place of the gods'), attested by 822 CE after the establishment of the Jokhang temple.

historical_names.name: Rasa
historical_names.source: Old Tibetan inscriptions (Skar cung Pillar, c. 800–815 CE) and 7th-century Jokhang foundation tradition (641 CE)
historical_names.notes: Originally known as Rasa ('goat's place') from the 7th century CE before being renamed Lhasa by 822 CE.

b_samye.first_mention_attestation: Founded between 763 and 779 CE (Testament of Ba records foundation in a hare year, 763 or 775 CE, and first monks ordained in 779 CE) under King Trisong Detsen.
b_samye.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Bsam yas (བསམ་ཡས, 'Inconceivable'), Tibet's first Buddhist monastery founded under Trisong Detsen in the late 8th century CE.

b_doilungdeqen.first_mention_attestation: Formed in the mid-14th century CE (c. 1350 CE) when the Dêqên ('Great Bliss') lamasery was built in Donggar and combined with the local name Doilung ('upper valley').
b_doilungdeqen.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Stod lung bde chen (སྟོད་ལུང་བདེ་ཆེན), combining 'upper valley' (Doilung) with the 14th-century Dêqên monastery.

b_quxu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern town and county (ཆུ་ཤུར, Chushur/Qüxü) at the confluence of the Lhasa and Yarlung Tsangpo rivers.
b_quxu.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Chu shur (ཆུ་ཤུར, 'water ditch'), referring to the settlement at the Lhasa–Yarlung Tsangpo confluence.

b_lhunzhub.first_mention_attestation: Established as Lhünzhub Dzong (ལྷུན་གྲུབ་རྫོང) in 1857 CE; merged with Pundo Dzong in 1959 CE.
b_lhunzhub.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Lhun grub (ལྷུན་གྲུབ, 'spontaneously accomplished'), established as a dzong in 1857 CE.

b_ngarnang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern village and township (ངར་ནང) in Lhünzhub County, Lhasa.
b_ngarnang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Ngar nang (ངར་ནང), modern rural township in Lhünzhub County.

b_reting.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1056 CE by Dromtönpa (1005–1064 CE), chief disciple of Atiśa, as the first monastery of the Kadampa school.
b_reting.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Rwa sgreng (རྭ་སྒྲེང, 'Radreng/Reting'), Kadampa monastery founded in 1056 CE north of Lhasa.

b_nyemo.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written or epigraphic attestation <= 867 CE; later Tibetan Buddhist hagiographies retrospectively cite Snye mo as the 8th-century CE birthplace of the translator Vairocana.
b_nyemo.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Snye mo (སྙེ་མོ, 'wheat'), an ancient agricultural district on the border of Ü and Tsang.

b_qewa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; constituent holding of Nyêmo in Lhasa Prefecture.
b_qewa.etymology_analysis: Tibetan local toponym in the Nyêmo valley of uncertain classical orthography, unattested before 867 CE.

b_pukpa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern settlement (Pukpa / Phubu, ཕུ་བུར) in Baingoin County, Nagqu.
b_pukpa.etymology_analysis: Tibetan pastoral toponym in Baingoin County (KNAB records Phubu/Pukpa/Pubur), unattested <= 867 CE.

b_xenkyer.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern township (Xênkyêr, ཤེ་འཁྱེར, Xinji) in Baingoin County, Nagqu, organized administratively in 1960 CE.
b_xenkyer.etymology_analysis: Tibetan She 'khyer (ཤེ་འཁྱེར), pastoral township in Baingoin County, Nagqu.

b_balla.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; constituent pastoral settlement in Baingoin County, Nagqu.
b_balla.etymology_analysis: Tibetan local pastoral toponym in the Baingoin/Namru area of Nagqu, unattested before 867 CE.

b_lhari.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern town and county seat (ལྷ་རི, 'Sacred Mountain') in Nagqu.
b_lhari.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Lha ri (ལྷ་རི, 'Sacred Mountain' or 'God Mountain'), naming the town and county in Nagqu.

b_codoi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern township (ཚོ་སྟོད, 'Upper Division') in Lhari County, Nagqu.
b_codoi.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Tsho stod (ཚོ་སྟོད, 'Upper Division'), directional/administrative subdivision name in Lhari County.

b_lingti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern township (གླིང་མཐིལ, 'Forest/Sanctuary Floor') in Lhari County, Nagqu.
b_lingti.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Gling mthil (གླིང་མཐིལ, glossed as 'forest embankment' or 'sanctuary base'), township in Lhari County.

b_nagchu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; Tibetan hydronym (ནག་ཆུ, 'Black River') for the upper Salween region, administered as Nagqu in the modern era.
b_nagchu.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Nag chu (ནག་ཆུ, 'Black River'), derived from the upper Salween River flowing through northern Tibet.

b_lhomar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern town (ལྷོ་དམར, Lhomar/Luoma) in Nagqu.
b_lhomar.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Lho dmar (ལྷོ་དམར, 'South Red'), directional compound naming a town in Nagqu.

b_taksar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern township (སྟག་གསར, Taksar/Dasa) in Nagqu.
b_taksar.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Stag gsar (སྟག་གསར, 'New Tiger'), modern township in Nagqu.

b_qangma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern town (བྱང་མ, 'Northern') in Nagqu.
b_qangma.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Byang ma (བྱང་མ, 'Northern'), directional compound naming a town in Nagqu.

b_comai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern county and town (མཚོ་སྨད, 'Lower Lake') in Shannan.
b_comai.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Mtsho smad (མཚོ་སྨད, 'Lower Lake'), directional/locator compound in Shannan.

b_lhozhag.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; first prominent in the 11th century CE (c. 1041 CE) with Marpa Lotsawa's foundation of Lo Drowolung Monastery in Lhozhag (ལྷོ་བྲག).
b_lhozhag.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Lho brag (ལྷོ་བྲག, 'Southern Cliff'), directional/locator compound in southern Shannan.

b_gyaca.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern county and town (རྒྱ་ཚ) on the Yarlung Tsangpo in Shannan.
b_gyaca.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Rgya tsha (རྒྱ་ཚ), settlement and county along the middle Yarlung Tsangpo in Shannan.

b_daklha_gampo.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1121 CE by Je Gampopa (1079–1153 CE) as Daklha Gampo Monastery (དྭགས་ལྷ་སྒམ་པོ), cradle of the Dakpo Kagyu lineage.
b_daklha_gampo.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Dwags lha sgam po (དྭགས་ལྷ་སྒམ་པོ), monastery founded in 1121 CE in Dakpo (Gyaca area).

b_sangri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern county and town (ཟངས་རི, 'Copper Mountain') in Shannan.
b_sangri.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Zangs ri (ཟངས་རི, 'Copper Mountain'), an oronym naming the town and county in Shannan.

b_nagarze.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern county and town (སྣ་དཀར་རྩེ, 'White Nose Peak') beside Yamdrok Lake in Shannan.
b_nagarze.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Sna dkar rtse (སྣ་དཀར་རྩེ, 'White Nose Peak'), an oronym referring to a white rocky promontory.

b_gonggar.first_mention_attestation: First rose to prominence in the mid-14th century CE (c. 1350 CE) with the establishment of Gonggar Dzong under the Phagmodrupa regime and later Gonggar Choide Monastery.
b_gonggar.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Gong dkar (གོང་དཀར, 'high white'), medieval Phagmodrupa stronghold in Shannan.

b_nang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern county and town (སྣང, Nang) on the lower Yarlung Tsangpo in Nyingchi.

morphemes.translation: light, appearance (locally associated with elephant-trunk topography)

b_nang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Snang (སྣང), town and county in Nyingchi along the Yarlung Tsangpo.

b_gedang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern Tibetan township (དགུ་ཐང, Guthang/Gedang) in Nyingchi.
b_gedang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Dgu thang (དགུ་ཐང, 'Nine Plains'), rendered in Chinese as Gedang.

b_zetang.first_mention_attestation: The town of Tsetang/Zetang (རྩེད་ཐང) dates to the founding of Tsetang Gompa in 1351 CE as a major center of learning in the Yarlung Valley.
b_zetang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Rtsed thang (རྩེད་ཐང, 'Playground'), named after the origin myth of the Tibetan people on nearby Mount Gongpori.

historical_names.name: Nedong
historical_names.source: Tibetan imperial-era records of Lower Yarlung (Sne-gdong of Lower Yarlung)
historical_names.notes: Sne-gdong (Nedong) in Lower Yarlung was an ancient imperial stronghold in the immediate area prior to the 1351 CE founding of Tsetang.

b_taktse.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Old Tibetan Annals (7th–8th century CE) as Chingwa Taktsé (ཕྱིང་བ་སྟག་རྩེ), the ancestral fortress of the Yarlung Tibetan emperors.
b_taktse.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Stag rtse (སྟག་རྩེ, 'Tiger Peak'), referring to Chingwa Taktsé, the ancient royal citadel of the Yarlung kings.

b_yumbu_lakhang.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written or epigraphic attestation <= 867 CE; later post-imperial Tibetan chronicles (12th–14th century CE) retrospectively attribute the palace to legendary first king Nyatri Tsenpo (traditionally 127 BCE) and 7th-century CE Songtsen Gampo.
b_yumbu_lakhang.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Yum bu bla sgang (ཡུམ་བུ་བླ་སྒང, 'Mother/Doe Upper Ridge Palace'), revered as the oldest palace in Tibet.

b_tradruk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 7th century CE (c. 641 CE) under King Songtsen Gampo as one of Tibet's earliest royal geomantic Buddhist temples, and listed among the three royal monasteries under Trisong Detsen (755–797 CE).
b_tradruk.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Khra 'brug (ཁྲ་འབྲུག, 'Hawk and Dragon'), commemorating the legend of Songtsen Gampo subduing a five-headed dragon in the form of a falcon.

b_qusum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in written sources <= 867 CE; modern county and town (ཆུ་གསུམ, 'Three Rivers') in Shannan.
b_qusum.etymology_analysis: Tibetan Chu gsum (ཆུ་གསུམ, 'Three Rivers'), a hydronym naming the town and county in Shannan.
